title: Paid the other driver privately, then the solicitor’s letter came
type: Late notification after a private settlement fell through
story: Policyholder notified the claim on 14 October, more than five months after a low-speed rear-end collision on 2 May at traffic lights on Fabian Way, Swansea. At the scene he agreed with the other driver to pay for her repairs himself to protect his no-claims discount, and paid £650 by bank transfer. On 9 October he received a letter from her solicitors notifying whiplash claims for her and her passenger, and asking for more money for the repairs.
statement: It was a tap in the queue at the lights, my fault, I'll say that straight away. She seemed fine and we agreed I'd sort her bumper so I didn't lose my no-claims. I paid what her garage asked. I never thought I'd hear any more about it. Now a solicitor says both of them were injured and the bumper cost more. I didn't tell you before because I didn't think there was anything to tell.

accounts.text: We act for Ms Leanne Morgan and her passenger Mr Kieran Morgan following a collision on 2 May at Fabian Way, Swansea. Both suffered whiplash injuries. Claims have been submitted through the Official Injury Claim portal. Our client also claims the balance of her repairs, £1,140, and 12 days of car hire. Please confirm your insurer's details within 21 days.
Transfer of £650.00 on 6 May from G Pryce to L Morgan, reference "bumper Fabian Way". No further payments between the two accounts.

whatHappened: A genuine low-speed rear-end collision for which he was at fault. He settled the damage privately to protect his discount and did not tell his insurer until the solicitor's letter arrived.
damage: Policyholder's Corsa: minor scuff to the front bumper, not claimed. Third party's Fiesta: rear bumper, £650 already paid privately; a further £1,140 and hire now claimed.
thirdParties: Leanne Morgan, driver of the Fiesta
evidence: Policyholder's photos of the Fiesta's bumper taken at the scene
missing: Medical reports for either injury claimant
The garage's invoice for the original repair
Messages exchanged with Ms Morgan after the accident
inconsistencies: The policyholder says Ms Morgan seemed uninjured at the scene; the solicitors say both occupants were injured
indicators: Injury claims arriving five months after a low-speed impact with no injury mentioned at the scene
Repair costs rising after a private settlement
innocent: Soft-tissue symptoms often appear a day or two after a collision
Drivers commonly settle small bumps privately to protect a no-claims discount, without realising the policy requires every incident to be reported
questions: Ask the policyholder for his scene photos, his messages with Ms Morgan and her garage's original quote
Ask whether the passenger was in the car and whether anyone mentioned pain at the scene
steps: Register the claim and take over the third-party claims now: late notice breaches the claims condition, but it does not remove the cover third parties rely on
Check whether the delay has prejudiced the insurer, for example lost evidence or costs that could have been avoided
Respond to the injury claims within the portal time limits and ask for the medical evidence
Give credit for the £650 already paid when settling the property claim
assessment: Genuine, at fault, notified late. The late notice and the private deal breach the policy conditions but the prejudice looks limited. The injury claims need the normal scrutiny given the low speed and the five-month gap, not an assumption of fraud.
action: Take over the third-party claims, investigate the injuries in the normal way, and remind the policyholder that every incident must be reported.
outcomes: Property settled with credit for the £650; injury claims settled at the tariff after medical reports
Passenger claim withdrawn when no medical evidence is produced

title: A claims firm that says it acts for him, and a signature he says is not his
type: Claim notified by a claims management firm without the policyholder’s authority
story: Insurer received an email from Apex Accident Assist saying it acts for the policyholder after a collision on the A40 in Oxford. It attached a signed authority form and asked the insurer to pay storage of £45 a day and release the car to its partner garage for repair. When the claims team called the policyholder, he said he had never heard of the firm. A recovery truck had stopped at the scene and taken his car "for safety", and the driver had asked for his details for the paperwork.
statement: Another car clipped my side as it came out of a petrol station. We swapped details. A tow truck pulled up within five minutes, I thought my breakdown cover had sent it. The driver took my licence photo and had me sign something on his phone screen, he said it was the tow receipt. I never asked anyone to make a claim for me. I want my car back and I don't want to pay storage to anyone.

accounts.text: Client: O. Adeyemi. I authorise Apex Accident Assist to act on my behalf in all matters arising from the accident on the A40, to arrange recovery, storage and repairs, and to receive payment. Signed electronically at 16:52, the time stamped as 18 minutes after the collision.
No call received from this member on the date of the accident. No recovery dispatched.

whatHappened: A genuine minor collision. An unsolicited recovery operator took the car and passed the policyholder's details to a claims firm, which is trying to build storage and repair charges against the insurer without his real consent.
damage: Policyholder's Golf: nearside doors scraped and dented. Storage invoice from the claims firm's yard: 6 days at £45 so far and rising.
thirdParties: The driver who came out of the petrol station
evidence: Authority form with an electronic signature
Photos of the damage taken by the policyholder
missing: The recovery operator's identity and trading name
The other driver’s insurer
The device record behind the electronic signature
inconsistencies: The form says he authorised a claims firm; he says he signed a tow receipt
indicators: Recovery truck at the scene within minutes without being called
Authority signed on a phone 18 minutes after the crash
Daily storage running at a yard the policyholder did not choose
innocent: Some recovery operators are called by police or passers-by; he may genuinely have signed a form he did not read
questions: Ask the policyholder to confirm in writing that he did not instruct the firm and wants the insurer to deal with the claim
Ask the firm for the full signed record, its regulatory authorisation and the basis of its storage charges
steps: Treat the policyholder as the customer and get his instructions directly, not through the claims firm
Do not pay storage or release the car to the firm until its authority is proved; arrange collection of the car to an approved repairer with the policyholder’s consent
Record how his personal data reached the firm and consider whether a data protection complaint is needed
Share the pattern with the counter-fraud team if the firm or the recovery operator appears on other claims
assessment: The accident looks genuine; the claims firm's involvement does not. The signature was obtained at the roadside under a misleading description, so the authority is doubtful and the storage charges should not be accepted.
action: Deal with the policyholder directly, move the car, refuse the storage and refer the firm's conduct to the counter-fraud team.
outcomes: Car moved to an approved repairer; the firm withdraws its storage invoice
Firm linked to other roadside sign-ups and reported

title: Borrowed a friend’s Golf, and his own policy did not follow him
type: Driving-other-cars extension used on a car that was not insured
story: Policyholder was driving a friend's Volkswagen Golf in Reading to collect a takeaway when he clipped a parked delivery van while pulling into a space. He has comprehensive cover on his own car with a driving-other-cars extension and has claimed under it for the van's damage. A check of the Motor Insurance Database shows the friend's own policy on the Golf lapsed three weeks before the accident.
statement: My policy says I can drive other cars, third party only, so I didn't think twice. Jamie said the car was fine to use. I had no idea his insurance had run out, he never mentioned it. I left a note on the van and called the number on the side straight away. I just want the van fixed, it was completely my fault.

accounts.text: You may drive a private car that does not belong to you and is not hired to you, with the owner's permission, for third-party cover only, provided the car is insured by its owner under a separate policy and you hold a full licence.
Golf registration: no current insurance record. Previous policy ended 21 days before the accident date. No continuous insurance enforcement letter yet issued.

whatHappened: A genuine low-speed parking collision. He relied on an extension that only applies when the borrowed car is itself insured, and neither he nor the owner checked.
damage: Delivery van: nearside rear corner panel and light, estimate £1,450. Golf: front bumper scuffed.
thirdParties: Jamie Fenwick, owner of the Golf
evidence: Photo of the note he left on the van
missing: The Golf owner's lapse notice from his former insurer
Confirmation from the van owner of how they want to claim
innocent: Many drivers believe the extension covers any car they borrow with permission
questions: Ask the Golf owner when he knew his policy had ended
Ask the van owner whether they hold their own cover and have claimed under it
steps: Confirm the extension’s condition that the borrowed car must be insured, and that it is not met here
Decline cover under the extension in writing, explaining the condition plainly
Explain the route for the van owner: their own policy or the Motor Insurers’ Bureau for an uninsured vehicle, and check whether the insurer has any role under the MIB arrangements before closing
Tell the policyholder that driving without valid cover may lead to enforcement and that he should not drive the Golf again
assessment: Genuine accident, honest driver, no cover. The extension only works when the borrowed car is insured, so the van's damage is not covered under his policy.
action: Decline under the extension with a clear explanation and point the van owner to the right route.
outcomes: Declined; the van owner claims from their own insurer, which recovers from the drivers
Complaint to the Financial Ombudsman not upheld because the condition is clear

title: Cancelled for a missed payment, by a notice she says never arrived
type: Collision two days after a cancellation for non-payment
story: Policyholder pays her premium monthly by direct debit. The July instalment was returned unpaid. The insurer's system shows a seven-day notice of cancellation issued by email on 18 July and the policy cancelled on 26 July. On 28 July she was in a collision at a junction in Leicester and called to claim, and was told she had no cover. She says she received no notice and that the payment failed because her bank changed her account number.
statement: My bank moved me to a new account in July and told me direct debits would carry over. Nobody told me one had failed. I've had no email and no letter. I check my email every day. If you'd told me I'd have paid the same afternoon. I've been with you for four years and never missed anything. The other driver went into the back of me, it wasn't even my fault.

accounts.text: 18 July 09:14: notice of cancellation for non-payment sent by email to priya.chauhan@gmial.com. 18 July 09:15: delivery failure returned, address not found. No letter generated: customer's preference set to email only. 26 July: policy cancelled.
If an instalment is not paid we may cancel your policy by giving you seven days' notice in writing to the email or postal address we hold for you.

whatHappened: A collision in which she was probably not at fault, two days after a cancellation whose notice never reached her because of a mistyped email address on her record.
damage: Her Corolla: rear bumper, boot lid and rear panel, estimate £3,200. The other car: front end damage.
thirdParties: The driver who hit her at the junction
evidence: Communications log with the failed delivery
Bank's letter about the account change
missing: Who entered the email address and when
The other driver's insurer and account of the collision
inconsistencies: The insurer says notice was given; its own log shows the notice was never delivered
innocent: A bank account switch can stop a direct debit without the customer knowing
A mistyped email domain would explain why nothing arrived
questions: Ask the policyholder for the bank’s account change letter
Check when the email address on file was last confirmed by her
steps: Review whether the cancellation was valid: the notice bounced and no letter was sent, so she may never have been given notice as the terms require
If notice was not validly given, treat the policy as in force on 28 July, take the unpaid instalment, and handle the claim
Pursue the other driver’s insurer for her losses if she was not at fault
Fix the record and check for other customers affected by the same failure mode
assessment: Disputed cover, but the evidence favours the customer: notice was never delivered and the insurer knew it the same minute. Relying on that cancellation would be hard to defend and unfair.
action: Reinstate cover for the date of the accident, collect the missed instalment and handle the claim.
outcomes: Cover reinstated; claim handled and recovered from the other driver’s insurer
Root-cause fix: bounced cancellation notices now trigger a letter

title: A learner, her brother in the passenger seat, and two years too few
type: Learner driver supervised by someone who did not meet the legal requirements
story: Policyholder is 17 and holds a provisional licence and a learner driver policy. While practising reversing into a bay at a retail park in Norwich she struck a parked Kia, damaging both cars. Her supervisor was her brother, aged 22, who passed his test two years and four months before the accident. The policy requires the supervisor to meet the legal conditions for supervising a learner.
statement: My brother's been driving for ages and he's really careful, Mum couldn't come that day. I misjudged the turn and the back corner went into the Kia. We waited for the owner and gave our details. I didn't know there was a rule about how long he'd had his licence. Will I lose my cover?

accounts.who: DVLA licence check of the supervisor
accounts.text: Full licence category B issued 2 years and 4 months before the accident date. Age 22. No endorsements.
You are covered only while you are supervised by a person aged 21 or over who has held a full UK licence for that type of vehicle for at least three years.

whatHappened: A genuine low-speed reversing accident. Her supervisor was over 21 but had not held his licence for the three years the law and the policy require.
damage: Her Fiesta: rear bumper and light, £900. Parked Kia: front wing and bumper, £1,700.
evidence: DVLA check of the brother's licence
missing: Whether a qualified supervisor was available that day
innocent: Many families do not know the three-year rule
questions: Confirm who was supervising and that the licence details are his
steps: Decline her own repairs: the supervision condition was not met

Handle the Kia owner’s claim: the insurer’s duties to third parties under the Road Traffic Act are wider than its own cover, and the policy may give a right to recover the outlay from the policyholder
Explain plainly why the own damage is not covered and what qualifies as a supervisor in future
assessment: Genuine accident, careless but honest. The supervision condition is a clear legal requirement and it was not met, so her own damage is not covered; the third party should not suffer for it.
action: Decline own damage, pay the Kia owner and consider recovery, with a clear explanation to the family.
outcomes: Kia owner paid; recovery of £1,700 agreed in instalments
Recovery waived after a hardship review

title: A winter in Alicante, and the 90-day limit in the small print
type: Collision abroad after the period of full cover in Europe had run out
story: Policyholder took his car on the ferry to Santander on 2 January to spend the winter near Alicante. On 15 April, 104 days later, he collided with a Spanish driver's Seat on a roundabout and has claimed for both cars. His schedule gives comprehensive cover in the EU for up to 90 days in any one period of insurance, then the minimum cover required by law in the country visited. He flew home for a week in March but the car stayed in Spain.
statement: The broker told me I was fully covered in Europe. I came home in March for my grandson's christening, so I thought the 90 days started again when I went back. The Spanish lady was very nice, we filled in the blue and yellow form together. I pulled onto the roundabout and misjudged her speed. My car needs a new wing and headlamp.

accounts.text: Completed and signed by both drivers at the roundabout. Vehicle B (policyholder) entering the roundabout; vehicle A already on it. Both boxes ticked consistent with B failing to give way. Sketch agrees.
Portsmouth to Santander, 2 January, one car and one passenger. Return sailing booked for 30 April.

whatHappened: A genuine roundabout collision abroad, after the 90 days of comprehensive cover in the period of insurance had been used up.
damage: His Qashqai: front wing, headlamp and bumper, about £3,900. The Seat: rear door and quarter panel.
missing: The broker's notes of what he was told about cover abroad
innocent: A trip home without the car could easily be mistaken for the start of a new trip
questions: Ask the broker for its record of the advice given
Confirm the dates the car was in Spain
steps: Handle the Spanish driver’s claim: the minimum legal cover still applies after the 90 days
Decline his own repairs: the 90 days run per period of insurance, not per trip, and were used up
If the broker told him he was fully covered, explain how to complain to the broker
assessment: Genuine collision abroad. Third-party cover still applies at the legal minimum, but comprehensive cover had ended after 90 days in the period of insurance.
action: Pay the Spanish third party, decline own damage with a clear explanation of the wording, and point him to the broker about the advice.
outcomes: Third party paid; own damage declined
Broker pays part of his repairs after a complaint about the advice

title: Three nurses, one car, and £20 each for petrol
type: Car-share passengers injured; hire-and-reward exclusion queried
story: Policyholder drives two colleagues to the hospital in Bristol for their early shifts, and each gives her £20 a week towards fuel. In fog she pulled out of a side road into the path of a van; both passengers were injured. The claims handler noted the weekly payments and asked whether the policy's exclusion for carrying passengers for hire or reward applies.
statement: We all live on the same estate and work the same shifts, so I drive. The girls give me £20 a week each, it doesn't even cover the diesel, I worked it out once. I didn't see the van in the fog, I looked twice. Ngozi hurt her neck and Sam broke her wrist on the door. I feel terrible.

accounts.who: Fuel and mileage note from the policyholder
accounts.text: Round trip 31 miles, five days a week, about 155 miles a week. Diesel about £27 a week, plus servicing and tyres. Contributions £40 a week in total, agreed before the arrangement started.
She came out of the side road right in front of me. Visibility was poor, maybe fifty metres, and I had my lights on. I braked but I couldn't stop.

whatHappened: A genuine junction collision in fog for which she was at fault. The fuel money is a car-sharing contribution towards running costs, not a fare.
damage: Her Octavia: front end and nearside wing. Van: nearside side panels. Passengers: a neck sprain and a fractured wrist.
evidence: Photos of the junction and vehicles
Hospital discharge note for the wrist fracture
missing: Medical reports for both passengers
innocent: Regular payments between colleagues can look like fares until the running costs are worked out
questions: Confirm the contributions were agreed before the journeys began and do not exceed the running costs
steps: Apply section 150 of the Road Traffic Act 1988: car-sharing contributions that do not exceed running costs, in a car carrying no more than eight passengers and arranged before the journey, are not hire or reward
Confirm cover and handle the passengers’ injury claims and the van owner’s claim
Record the reasoning so the exclusion is not raised again on renewal
assessment: Genuine and covered. The payments are a car-sharing contribution below the running costs, which the law treats as outside the hire-and-reward exclusion.
action: Confirm cover, accept liability for the junction collision and handle both injury claims and the van.
outcomes: Cover confirmed; injury claims settled
Policyholder reassured and keeps the car share

title: The supplement after the strip-down, and the rust behind the wing
type: Hidden damage found on strip-down, mixed with older corrosion
story: Policyholder slid into a stone gatepost in the rain on a farm track near Brecon. The first estimate, agreed from photos, was £2,800 for the bumper, headlamp and wing. After strip-down the repairer asked for a supplement of £3,600 for the nearside chassis leg, inner wing and radiator support. Strip-down photos show a kinked chassis leg with fresh bare metal, and an inner wing with rust holes and old filler.
statement: I took the corner too fast and the front corner hit the gatepost, it was quite a bang. The garage rang and said there's more damage underneath. The car's eleven years old, I know it's not perfect, but it drove fine before. I just want it put back how it was.

accounts.text: On strip-down: nearside chassis leg kinked 40 mm, requires section repair. Inner wing damaged and corroded, recommend replacement. Radiator support cracked at the mounting. Additional £3,600 including jig time.
Advisory recorded 2 years before the accident: "Nearside front inner wing corroded." Same advisory 1 year before. No advisories for the chassis leg or radiator support.

whatHappened: A genuine impact that bent the chassis leg and cracked the radiator support. The corroded inner wing was already failing and its replacement is partly old wear, not crash damage.
damage: Kuga: bumper, headlamp, wing, chassis leg, radiator support, and an inner wing that is both damaged and corroded. Agreed £2,800 plus £3,600 requested.
missing: An engineer's inspection of the inner wing
Close-up photos of the chassis leg fracture surfaces
inconsistencies: The repairer lists the inner wing as crash damage; the MOT history shows it was corroded for two years
indicators: Supplement larger than the original estimate
Old corrosion presented as crash damage
innocent: Hidden damage behind a front corner impact is common and photos cannot show it
The repairer may simply have recommended the inner wing because it cannot be welded to sound metal
questions: Ask the repairer for close-ups of the inner wing and the chassis leg
Ask the engineer whether the inner wing could be repaired locally once the corrosion is cut out
steps: Send an engineer to inspect before authorising the supplement
Accept the chassis leg and radiator support as crash damage
Treat the corroded inner wing as betterment or wear: pay only for the crash-related part of the work
Recheck whether the total now makes the car uneconomical to repair
assessment: Mixed. The impact was genuine and the hidden damage is mostly real, but the corroded inner wing pre-dates the accident and should not be paid in full.
action: Inspect, approve the crash-related supplement and agree a contribution for the corroded inner wing.
outcomes: Supplement approved at £2,450 after the inner wing is split
Car declared uneconomical to repair when the total passes its value

title: A new exhaust and four tyres after one kerb
type: Betterment on parts that were worn before the accident
story: Policyholder lost grip on a frosty morning in Perth and slid sideways into a high kerb at low speed. The nearside wheels, two tyres and the exhaust were damaged. Her garage replaced the whole exhaust system, all four tyres and the nearside wheels. The insurer's assessor has deducted a betterment contribution from the invoice, and she has phoned to complain.
statement: It's a 2012 Jazz with 160,000 miles on it and it's my lifeline, I care for my mum. The garage said the exhaust was knackered anyway and they couldn't fit just the middle section, so they did the lot. They said you should never have two new tyres and two old ones. Why should I pay for any of it when the ice did this?

accounts.text: Full exhaust system £640, of which middle section damaged by impact. Two nearside alloy wheels £420. Four tyres £380: two nearside damaged, two offside at 2 mm tread. Labour £210.
Front and rear exhaust sections heavily corroded before the incident. Offside tyres not damaged. Betterment applied: £330 for the exhaust sections not damaged, offside tyres removed from the claim.

whatHappened: A genuine low-speed slide into a kerb. Part of the repair replaced worn parts that were not damaged, which put the car in a better state than before.
damage: Jazz: two nearside wheels and tyres, exhaust middle section. Worn but undamaged: exhaust front and rear sections, two offside tyres.
evidence: Photos of the exhaust and the tyres
missing: Whether the middle exhaust section was available on its own
innocent: Garages often replace worn neighbouring parts to give a sound repair
questions: Ask the garage whether a middle section alone was available and at what price
steps: Pay for the parts the accident damaged: the two wheels, two tyres and the exhaust section
Explain the betterment clearly: the undamaged worn sections and tyres were replaced by choice
If a middle section could not be bought alone, reduce or drop the exhaust contribution
Note her caring responsibilities and handle the complaint promptly
assessment: Genuine claim; a fair betterment question. The worn tyres should not be paid, but the exhaust contribution depends on whether a partial repair was really possible.
action: Pay the damaged parts, keep the tyre deduction, and recheck the exhaust contribution with the garage.
outcomes: Exhaust contribution dropped when no middle section was available; tyre deduction kept
Complaint closed with an explanation she accepts

title: Agreed at £24,000, offered £17,500
type: Total loss of a classic car on an agreed value policy
story: Policyholder's 1972 Triumph Stag was written off when a tractor pulled out of a field entrance into its side on a lane near Ludlow. The car is insured on an agreed value policy at £24,000, set at inception from an owners' club valuation with photographs. The insurer's total loss team has offered £17,500, based on recent auction results for similar cars.
statement: I've owned her for nineteen years. We agreed the value with you three years ago, you had the club's report and thirty photos. Nothing about the car changed since then except it got better, I had the hood replaced. Why am I being offered auction prices now? The tractor driver admitted it at the scene.

accounts.text: Agreed value: £24,000. Basis of settlement for a total loss: the agreed value shown in the schedule, less any excess. Valuation report and photographs held on file at inception.
I was coming out of the gate and the hedge blocks the view. I edged out and didn't see him. My fault, I've told my boss and our insurer.

whatHappened: A genuine collision caused by the tractor. The car is a total loss and the policy pays the agreed value, not a market value.
damage: Stag: chassis and offside body crushed, total loss. Tractor: minor scrape to the front weight.
thirdParties: Farm that owns the tractor and its insurer
evidence: Policy schedule with the agreed value
Club valuation and photos from inception
missing: The farm insurer's acknowledgement of liability
inconsistencies: The settlement offer uses auction values; the policy promises the agreed value
innocent: A total loss team may have applied the standard market value process by mistake
questions: Ask whether anything about the car has changed since the valuation that would affect the agreed value
steps: Settle at the agreed value less the excess, as the schedule says
Pursue the farm’s insurer for the outlay; liability is admitted
Offer the policyholder the chance to retain the salvage at an agreed deduction if he wants to rebuild
Find out why the agreed value basis was missed and fix the process
assessment: Genuine and straightforward on cover. The agreed value binds the insurer unless something material changed or was misstated, and nothing suggests that.
action: Pay £24,000 less the excess and recover from the tractor's insurer.
outcomes: Agreed value paid; full recovery from the farm insurer
Policyholder retains the salvage for a rebuild

title: Paid out for the stolen RAV4, then the police found it
type: Stolen car recovered after the total loss settlement
story: Policyholder's Toyota RAV4 was stolen from her driveway in Solihull without the keys. After 30 days the insurer paid a total loss settlement of £27,400 and she bought another car. Seven weeks later police found the RAV4 in a lock-up in Coventry on false plates with a damaged ignition, a missing rear seat and scratched paintwork. She has asked whether she can have it back.
statement: I loved that car, it had my dad's old sat nav mount and everything. I've bought another car now but if I can get the RAV4 back for a sensible price I'd sell the new one. Does it belong to me or to you now? The police said to ring my insurer.

accounts.text: Vehicle identified by its chassis number in a lock-up with three other stolen vehicles. False registration plates fitted. Ignition barrel damaged, rear seat missing, paint scratched on both sides. Released to the owner's insurer on request.

Total loss settlement £27,400 paid to the policyholder 30 days after the theft. Signed form of discharge transfers the vehicle to the insurer on payment. Vehicle recorded on the theft register; register update pending.

whatHappened: A genuine theft. The car was recovered after the settlement, so it belongs to the insurer under the discharge she signed.
damage: RAV4: ignition barrel, missing rear seat, scratches to both sides; repair estimate about £3,100. False plates removed.
thirdParties: Owners of the other vehicles in the lock-up
missing: A full inspection for hidden damage or tampering with the chassis number
innocent: The forced ignition and false plates fit a professional theft for resale, not owner involvement
questions: Ask whether she wants to buy the car back and at what price she would consider it
steps: Confirm the chassis number and inspect the car for hidden damage and tampering
Explain that the car now belongs to the insurer under the signed discharge
Offer a buy-back at a fair figure reflecting the damage, or sell it through salvage if she declines
Update the theft register and the police so the car is no longer shown as stolen
assessment: Genuine theft, correctly settled. The recovered car is the insurer's; a fair buy-back offer is good customer treatment.
action: Inspect, update the register and offer her a buy-back.
outcomes: Bought back at £19,800 and repaired at her chosen garage
Sold at auction after she decides to keep her new car

title: Eight miles an hour, whiplash, and a travel anxiety uplift
type: Low-speed whiplash claim with a psychological element and loss of earnings
story: Our policyholder rolled into the back of Ms Brennan's car in slow traffic on Kirkstall Road, Leeds, at about 8 mph by his own account. Her representatives have submitted a whiplash claim through the Official Injury Claim portal for neck pain lasting 9 to 12 months with travel anxiety, ask for an uplift for exceptional circumstances, and claim £2,000 of lost earnings as a self-employed hairdresser.
statement: It was a proper jolt, my head went forward and back. My neck was stiff the next morning and I couldn't do colour work for weeks, it's all arms up. I get nervous in traffic now and I tense up when anyone's behind me. I had to turn clients away. I'm self-employed so if I don't work, I don't get paid.

accounts.text: Seen 7 weeks after the accident. Neck pain, moderate at first, now mild. Prognosis for the whiplash injury: 6 months from the accident. Reports anxiety as a passenger and driver in heavy traffic, expected to resolve within 3 months. No pre-existing neck problems reported.
The traffic was crawling and I looked down at the satnav. I touched her bumper, it barely moved her car. She got out, said she was fine and we swapped details. I've told my insurer it was my fault.

whatHappened: A genuine low-speed rear-end collision with a real but short-lived neck injury. The duration claimed and the lost earnings are overstated.
damage: Her Mini: rear bumper scuff, repaired for £420. Our policyholder's Astra: no visible damage.
thirdParties: Kelly Brennan, driver of the Mini
evidence: Screenshot of her salon's Instagram showing her at work styling a client's colour, posted two days after the accident
missing: Appointment book or invoices showing turned-away clients
Tax returns for the last two years
GP records
inconsistencies: She says she could not do colour work for weeks; the salon posted her doing colour work two days later
Claim says 9 to 12 months; the medical expert says 6 months
indicators: Duration claimed longer than the medical prognosis
Lost earnings claimed without business records
innocent: A post can be scheduled in advance or show a colleague’s work
Some people work through pain and pay for it later
questions: Ask her representatives for the appointment book, invoices and tax returns
Ask who posted the Instagram photo and who is in it
steps: Value the injury on the tariff using the medical prognosis, in the column for whiplash with minor psychological injury if the evidence supports it
Resist the uplift: an increase for exceptional circumstances is capped and needs evidence that the injury was exceptionally severe or its effects exceptional
Require business records before paying any lost earnings
Put the Instagram post to her representatives rather than alleging dishonesty outright
assessment: Genuine accident and a genuine minor injury, exaggerated in duration and financial effect. Pay the tariff the evidence supports; the uplift and the earnings claim are not proved.
action: Offer the tariff amount for a 6-month injury with the minor psychological element, and ask for proof of the lost earnings.
outcomes: Settled at tariff for 6 months; earnings claim dropped
Claimant accepts after the Instagram post is raised

title: A Polish artic on the M20, and whose blind spot it was
type: Lane change collision with a foreign-registered lorry
story: Policyholder says a Polish-registered articulated lorry moved from lane 1 into lane 2 of the M20 near Maidstone and pushed his BMW into the central barrier. The lorry driver stopped and gave his details and his insurer's name. The lorry's insurer has appointed a UK claims handling agent, which says its driver checked his mirrors and the BMW was accelerating in his blind spot.
statement: I was overtaking in lane 2 in the rain, doing about 65, steady. The lorry's indicator came on and it moved over at the same time, there was no gap. I braked and went left of the barrier, the trailer wheels caught my passenger side. My dashcam only faces forwards, but you can see the trailer come across.

accounts.who: Lorry driver, through the claims handling agent
accounts.text: I indicated and checked my mirrors three times. Lane 2 was clear. The car came very fast from behind and was in my blind spot when I started to move. I stopped on the hard shoulder and gave my details.

Trailer's rear lights visible ahead and to the left. Trailer moves into lane 2 over about 2 seconds, starting 0.6 seconds after its indicator first shows. Speed shown on the overlay: 64 mph, steady before braking.

whatHappened: A lane change by the lorry with too little time between indicating and moving. The policyholder was not speeding, but whether he was in the blind spot is genuinely disputed.
damage: BMW 3 Series: nearside doors, wheel and front wing, offside scraped along the barrier; estimate £7,800. Lorry trailer: scuffed side guard.
thirdParties: Lorry's insurer and its UK claims handling agent
evidence: Photos of the barrier and the car
missing: The lorry's own camera footage and tachograph record
The lorry's lane-change or blind-spot sensor data
inconsistencies: The driver says the car came very fast; the dashcam shows a steady 64 mph
innocent: Blind spots on the nearside of right-hand-drive cars passing a left-hand-drive lorry are a well-known hazard on both sides
questions: Ask the claims handling agent for the lorry's camera footage and tachograph download before they are overwritten
Ask the policyholder how long he had been alongside the trailer
steps: Claim against the lorry's insurer through its UK claims handling agent; if it had none, the Motor Insurers' Bureau acts for foreign vehicles in the UK
Ask now, in writing, for the lorry’s camera footage, tachograph and sensor data to be preserved
Pay the policyholder’s repairs under his comprehensive cover and recover the outlay
Expect the barrier repair to be claimed by National Highways from whoever is found liable
assessment: Disputed, but the dashcam supports the policyholder: the lorry moved 0.6 seconds after indicating and he was at a steady legal speed. Liability likely falls mostly or wholly on the lorry.
action: Pay the repairs, preserve the lorry's data and pursue a full recovery through the claims handling agent.
outcomes: Lorry footage confirms a late check; full recovery agreed
Settled 80/20 after the lorry footage shows the BMW alongside for several seconds

title: A nine-year-old between parked cars, and parents who want it settled quickly
type: Child pedestrian injury where the settlement needs court approval
story: Policyholder was driving past a primary school in Bradford at 15:20 when a nine-year-old boy ran out between parked cars. The boy suffered a broken shin and a cut that will scar. The policyholder's telematics box recorded 24 mph in a 20 mph zone at the moment of braking. The boy's parents have phoned the insurer asking for £8,000 now to settle everything, without solicitors.
statement: He came out from between two vans, I had no chance to see him. I braked hard. I know I was a bit over twenty. I went to the hospital the next day to see how he was. His dad was decent about it. They just want it over with, and so do I.

accounts.text: Speed 24 mph at the start of hard braking, 9 mph at impact, stopped 1.1 seconds later. Posted limit 20 mph. Time 15:20, school day.
Nine-year-old male. Closed fracture of the left tibia, treated in a cast. 4 cm laceration to the left knee, sutured, likely to scar. Follow-up in fracture clinic.

whatHappened: A genuine accident in which the driver was over the limit outside a school at home time, and a child was injured. Any settlement must protect the child.
damage: Child: fractured tibia and a scar. Policyholder's Kia: dent to the bonnet.
missing: A full medical report on the fracture and the scar
Witness accounts from other parents at the school gate
innocent: A child running out between parked vans may not have been avoidable even at 20 mph; the speed still weighs heavily on liability
questions: Ask the parents whether they have taken legal advice and explain why the court has to approve a child’s settlement
steps: Do not agree a settlement directly with the parents: an agreement for a child is only binding once the court approves it under Part 21 of the Civil Procedure Rules
Accept that primary liability is likely given the speed outside a school; a contributory negligence argument against a nine-year-old is weak
Get a full medical report, including on the scar, and offer an interim payment if the family has costs now
Diary the limitation position: time does not start to run until the child turns 18
assessment: Genuine and serious. Liability will probably rest with the driver. The parents' wish to settle quickly is understandable but cannot be met without court approval.
action: Accept liability in principle, fund medical evidence and any interim needs, and settle only through an approved settlement.
outcomes: Settlement of £14,500 approved by the court and invested for the child
Family instruct solicitors; approval hearing after the scar report

title: A Part 36 offer on the handler’s desk while she was on leave
type: Disputed cyclist injury claim with a time-limited settlement offer
story: A cyclist was injured when our policyholder's van turned left across her at a junction on Oxford Road, Manchester. The van driver says she rode up his inside as he turned. Her solicitors sent a Part 36 offer dated 3 March to settle for £38,000. The handler was on leave and the file was picked up on 20 March; nobody has responded.
statement: I was in the cycle lane going straight on. The van overtook me and then turned left right in front of me. I had nowhere to go. I broke my collarbone and two ribs and I was off work for three months. I've cycled that route for six years.

accounts.text: I was indicating left for a good while and checked my mirror before I turned. She must have come up the inside fast. I felt a bump and stopped straight away.
This offer is made under Part 36. Our client will accept £38,000 in settlement of her whole claim. The relevant period is 21 days from the date of this letter.

whatHappened: A left-turn collision with a cyclist going straight on in a cycle lane. Liability is disputed but the van driver's position is weak. A time-limited offer is about to expire.
damage: Cyclist: fractured collarbone and two ribs, three months off work. Bicycle written off. Van: no damage.
evidence: Photos of the junction showing the cycle lane
missing: Van camera footage
Nearby CCTV
A valuation of the claim from counsel or a senior handler
inconsistencies: The van driver says he indicated well before the turn; the cyclist says the van overtook her first
innocent: A cyclist close to the kerb in a cycle lane can be hidden from a van’s nearside mirror
questions: Ask the van operator for its camera footage
Ask how long the van was alongside the cyclist before turning
steps: Work out the deadline today: 21 days from 3 March is 24 March
Get the claim valued and liability reviewed before the deadline, including a realistic view of contributory negligence
Decide whether to accept, or make a well-judged Part 36 offer of the insurer’s own
Explain to the business why: if the claimant later beats her own offer at trial, the insurer faces enhanced interest, indemnity costs and an additional sum
Fix the diary process so offers are picked up when a handler is away
assessment: Disputed on paper, but liability is likely to fall mainly on the van. The urgent risk is procedural: an ignored Part 36 offer can cost far more than the claim.
action: Value the claim and respond to the offer before 24 March, with a counter-offer if £38,000 is too high.
outcomes: Settled at £33,500 after a counter-offer within the relevant period
Offer accepted after counsel advises it is within the likely range

title: Lent to a mate for the airport run, and only one name on the policy
type: Uninsured friend driving with permission; third parties paid and the outlay recovered
story: Policyholder's policy covers him as the only driver. He lent his car to a friend, who has no insurance of his own, to drive to Liverpool airport. In heavy rain the friend lost control on a bend, hit a bus shelter and a parked car. The council and the parked car's owner have both claimed against the policy, and the policyholder wants his own car repaired too.
statement: Ryan's a good driver, he's just never had his own car. It was one trip. I didn't think about the insurance, I thought it covered the car. I know it was stupid. Can you not just fix it and put my premium up?

accounts.text: The road was flooded on the bend and the back end went. I hit the shelter and slid into a parked Clio. Nobody was hurt. I don't have any insurance, Callum said it would be fine.
Persons entitled to drive: the policyholder only. Use: social, domestic and pleasure and commuting.

whatHappened: An uninsured friend drove with the policyholder's permission and crashed. The policy does not cover him, but the third parties must still be paid.
damage: Bus shelter: glass and frame, council estimate £3,600. Parked Clio: rear quarter and door, £2,900. Policyholder's Focus: front and side, £4,100.
missing: Police report, if one was made
innocent: Many people believe insurance follows the car rather than the driver
questions: Confirm the driver has no policy of his own that might give cover
steps: Decline the policyholder’s own repairs: the driver was not insured
Pay the council and the Clio owner: section 151 of the Road Traffic Act 1988 requires the insurer to meet third-party claims of this kind even though the driver was not covered
Recover the outlay from the person who permitted the use (the policyholder) or the driver, as section 151(8) allows, and agree a realistic repayment plan
Tell both men that driving without insurance is an offence
assessment: Genuine accident caused by an uninsured driver with permission. Third parties are protected by law; the policyholder's own damage is not covered and the insurer can recover what it pays.
action: Pay the third parties, decline own damage, and pursue recovery from the policyholder or the driver.
outcomes: £6,500 paid to third parties; recovery agreed at £150 a month
Recovery pursued against the driver after the policyholder shows hardship

title: The barrier came down on the roof, and the car park’s sign says not our problem
type: Car park barrier damage with an exclusion of liability in the operator’s terms
story: Policyholder was leaving a multi-storey car park in Nottingham when the exit barrier came down on her roof and windscreen. She had paid at the machine. The car park's CCTV shows her following the car in front closely through the raised barrier instead of waiting for it to reset. The operator says its displayed terms exclude all liability for damage to vehicles.
statement: I'd paid, the ticket was in my hand. The barrier went up for the car in front and stayed up, so I went. It came straight down on me. There's a sign saying don't follow other cars but I didn't see it until afterwards. Surely a barrier shouldn't come down on a car that's under it?

accounts.text: Our terms, displayed at the entrance, state that barriers may lower without warning, that drivers must not follow other vehicles, and that we accept no liability for damage to vehicles. We decline your claim.
Exit barrier 2: safety loop sensor fault reported two days before the incident; engineer visit booked for the following week. Barrier left in service.

whatHappened: She followed another car too closely, but the barrier's safety sensor was known to be faulty and the operator left it in service. Both share responsibility.
damage: Her Yaris: dented roof panel and cracked windscreen, estimate £1,850.
evidence: CCTV still showing the gap between the cars
missing: The operator's full terms and where they are displayed
innocent: Following through a raised barrier is a common mistake
questions: Ask the operator when the sensor was repaired
steps: Pay her repairs under her comprehensive cover, less her excess

Pursue the operator: a term excluding liability for negligence is subject to the fairness test in the Consumer Rights Act 2015, and leaving a barrier with a known sensor fault in service is strong evidence of negligence
Expect a deduction for her following too closely and settle the recovery on a shared basis
Seek her uninsured excess as part of the recovery
assessment: Genuine damage with shared fault. The exclusion sign is not the end of the matter: the known sensor fault makes a recovery worth pursuing, reduced for her tailgating.
action: Pay the claim and recover from the operator on a shared-liability basis.
outcomes: Operator pays 60% after the maintenance log is raised
Recovery abandoned after the operator shows the sensor was repaired the day before

title: A dashcam clip with the wrong font on its clock
type: Lane change claim supported by an edited dashcam video
story: Policyholder claims a delivery van drifted into his lane on the A13 in Essex and sideswiped his Audi, and has sent a 40-second dashcam clip that appears to show the van moving across. The van operator's insurer has sent its own forward and side camera footage, which shows the Audi changing lanes into the van. A digital forensics review of the policyholder's clip found signs of editing.
statement: The van came over on me, simple as that, it's all on my dashcam. I've sent you the clip. The van driver's lying to save his job. I want the other side to pay and I want my no-claims protected.

accounts.text: File re-encoded by consumer video editing software; original camera file names and GPS track absent. Frame rate drops from 30 to 24 for 3 seconds around the contact. Timestamp overlay uses a different typeface from this camera model's standard overlay. The clip cannot be relied on as an original recording.

Forward and nearside cameras, with GPS. Van steady in lane 1 at 52 mph. Audi enters lane 1 from lane 2 without indicating and makes contact with the van's offside front. Time and position match the reported accident.

whatHappened: The Audi cut into the van's lane. The policyholder's clip was edited to make the van appear to move across.
damage: Audi A4: nearside doors and wheel arch, estimate £4,300. Van: offside front wing and mirror.
missing: The dashcam's memory card and the original files
The make and model of the dashcam
inconsistencies: The policyholder's clip shows the van moving across; the van's own GPS-stamped cameras show the Audi moving across
indicators: Re-encoded file with no original metadata
Frame rate change around the moment of contact
Overlay typeface that does not match the camera model
innocent: Phones and apps sometimes re-encode video when files are shared, which strips metadata
questions: Ask the policyholder for the memory card and the original files from the camera
Ask how the clip was copied and sent
steps: Ask for the memory card before reaching any conclusion: an innocent re-encoding would not explain the frame rate change or the overlay typeface
Refer to the counter-fraud team with the forensics report and the van footage
Treat liability as resting on the policyholder on the current evidence and deal with the van operator’s claim
If editing is confirmed, decline the claim and consider the policy and reporting consequences of a fraudulent claim
assessment: Potential fraud with strong evidence. The independent van footage shows the policyholder at fault, and the clip he sent shows signs of deliberate editing.
action: Request the original files, refer to the counter-fraud team, and handle the van operator's claim against the policy.
outcomes: Memory card not produced; claim declined as fraudulent and policy cancelled
Policyholder withdraws his own claim and accepts fault

title: New bank details, from an email address one letter wrong
type: Attempt to divert a total loss settlement by impersonating the customer
story: A total loss settlement of £14,200 was due to the policyholder, aged 71, after her Honda was stolen and burnt out in Dundee. Two days before payment an email arrived from jean.fairbairn@outIook.com asking for the money to go to a new bank account "because my bank is moving my accounts", with a scanned letter. Her earlier emails came from jean.fairbairn@outlook.com. The handler had started to update the bank details.
statement: I haven't sent you any new bank details. My bank is the same bank I've had for forty years. I did get a phone call last week from someone saying they were from the insurance helping with my claim, and they knew all about the car. I told them when the money was coming. Have I done something wrong?

accounts.text: Earlier messages: sender jean.fairbairn@outlook.com, sent from a home broadband address in Dundee. New message: sender jean.fairbairn@outIook.com (capital I in place of the letter l), sent from a hosting provider abroad. Domain outIook.com registered nine days ago.
Name check on the new account: no match. Account holder name returned: J F Services Ltd.

whatHappened: A genuine claim. A fraudster who knew the claim details impersonated the customer to divert the settlement, probably after phoning her for information.
damage: Honda Jazz: stolen and burnt out, total loss settlement £14,200 due. No money lost yet.
evidence: Customer's account of the phone call
missing: How the caller knew the claim details
inconsistencies: The new email claims to be from the customer; she says she sent nothing
indicators: Look-alike email domain registered days ago
Request to change bank details just before payment
Payee name check fails
innocent: Genuine customers do change banks, which is why a change is verified with them rather than refused
questions: Ask the customer what she told the caller and whether she gave any security details
Check whether any other claim has had a similar request
steps: Stop the bank detail change and pay only to the account verified with the customer by phoning the number on file
Treat the customer as the victim: she has done nothing wrong and is now a target
Report the attempt to the fraud team and to Action Fraud, and check how the claim details leaked
Warn her about follow-up calls and offer to note a password for future contact
assessment: The claim is genuine and the customer is innocent. This is an outside attempt to divert her payment, stopped by the payee check.
action: Pay the settlement to her verified account, report the attempt and look for a data leak.
outcomes: Settlement paid safely; fraud reported
Investigation finds a compromised supplier mailbox and other customers are warned

title: Insured at 23:52, crashed at 22:14
type: Policy bought after an accident, with the time of the accident moved
story: Policyholder bought a policy online at 23:52 on 11 November for a 2016 Audi A3 that had had no insurance for two months. At 00:40 on 12 November he reported hitting a parked Ford Puma at 00:25 while turning into a street in Wolverhampton. The Puma's owner had called the police at 22:17 on 11 November, saying her doorbell camera had just recorded an Audi hitting her car, and gave the registration.
statement: It happened after midnight, about twenty past twelve. I clipped her car turning in and I went straight to my mate's to ring you. I'd sorted the insurance earlier that night. I don't know why she's saying a different time, maybe her camera clock is wrong.

accounts.text: Call received 22:17 on 11 November. Caller reports a dark Audi A3 has just struck her parked Puma and driven off; registration given from her doorbell camera, matching the policyholder's car.
Clip time-stamped 22:14:36 on 11 November. Audi hits the Puma's rear quarter while turning, pauses, then drives away. The camera's clock agrees with the network time on a later test.

whatHappened: He hit the parked car at 22:14 while uninsured, then bought a policy at 23:52 and reported the accident as happening after the policy started.
damage: Ford Puma: rear quarter panel and light, estimate £2,650. Audi: front corner scuffed.
missing: An account from the friend whose house he says he rang from
inconsistencies: He says the accident was at 00:25; the police log and camera show 22:14, before the policy was bought
indicators: Policy bought after two months without cover, less than an hour before the reported accident
Accident time moved to fall after the policy start
He left the scene
innocent: A camera clock can be wrong, but this one was tested and the police call was made at 22:17
questions: Put the police log and camera time to him in an interview under caution if the police take it on
steps: Decline the claim: the accident happened before the policy began, and the claim misstates the time
Treat the claim as fraudulent: the insurer can refuse it, end the policy from the time of the fraud and recover its costs
Tell the Puma owner the vehicle was not insured by this insurer at the time, so her claim falls to the Motor Insurers’ Bureau as an uninsured driver claim
Record the fraud on industry databases and share the evidence with the police
assessment: Confirmed fraud: independent, time-stamped evidence puts the accident 98 minutes before the policy was bought.
action: Decline, end the policy for fraud, direct the third party to the Motor Insurers' Bureau and report.
outcomes: Claim declined, policy cancelled; police charge him with driving without insurance and fraud
Third party paid by the Motor Insurers’ Bureau

title: A subject access request while the investigators are still working
type: Data access request during a fraud investigation of a theft claim
story: Policyholder claims his Range Rover Sport was stolen from a gym car park in Reading. The claim has been with the investigation unit for six weeks because one of the two keys has not been produced and the car's finance was in arrears. On 3 February he sent a subject access request asking for all his personal data, including investigators' notes, call recordings and "the real reason my claim is delayed".
statement: I've given you everything. The second key was lost years ago, I told you that. You've had investigators ringing my gym and my bank. I'm entitled to see what you're saying about me, it's the law. If I don't get it all within a month I'll go to the regulator.

accounts.text: Dated 3 February. Under the UK GDPR I request a copy of all personal data you hold about me, including notes, emails, call recordings, investigator reports and any data shared with third parties, and the reasons for the delay in my claim.
Enquiries ongoing with the finance company and a tracking provider. A witness statement from the gym is awaited. Disclosure of the investigation plan now would be likely to prejudice the enquiries.

whatHappened: A theft claim under genuine investigation. The data request is lawful and must be answered, but some investigation material can be withheld while disclosure would prejudice the enquiry.
damage: Range Rover Sport: reported stolen, value about £48,000; not recovered.
missing: The second key
The tracking provider’s report
indicators: One key missing
Finance in arrears before the theft
innocent: Keys are often lost over years of ownership
People in financial difficulty are also victims of theft
questions: Confirm his identity before releasing any data
steps: Log the request and diary the deadline: one month from receipt, 3 March
Disclose everything that is not exempt, including call recordings and correspondence
Withhold only the material whose disclosure would be likely to prejudice the prevention or detection of crime, using the crime exemption in the Data Protection Act 2018, and record why
Tell him that some information has been withheld under an exemption where that is allowed, and how to complain to the Information Commissioner
Keep the investigation moving: the data request does not pause it
assessment: Suspicious theft claim, legitimately under investigation, and a valid data access request that must be answered on time. The exemption allows narrow withholding, not a refusal.
action: Respond by 3 March with everything not exempt, withhold the investigation plan with a recorded reason, and continue the enquiries.
outcomes: Request answered on time with redactions; claim later paid after the tracker report
Claim declined after the second key is found in his car at a garage

title: His policy, her phone call, the week of the funeral
type: Claim reported by a bereaved spouse after the policyholder died in a collision
story: Policyholder died when a car crossed the central reservation of the A1 near Newark and struck his car head-on. The other driver survived and has been arrested. His wife, a named driver on the policy, called to report the claim the week of the funeral. She needs a car to take their three children to school and has asked what happens to the policy and the car.
statement: I'm sorry, I don't really know what I'm supposed to do. Everything is in David's name. The police have the car. People keep asking me for the death certificate and I've only got two copies. I need to get the kids to school next week. I can't keep telling the story.

accounts.text: Collision on the A1 southbound. Northbound vehicle crossed the central reservation. Other driver arrested on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving. Vehicle held for examination; will be released to the family's insurer when the examination is complete.
Policyholder: David Mensah. Named driver: Abena Mensah. Comprehensive. Renewal in four months. Monthly payments by direct debit from his account.

whatHappened: A fatal head-on collision caused by the other driver. The family is grieving and the policy is in the name of the man who died.
damage: Policyholder's Skoda: total loss, held by the police. Fatal injury to the policyholder.
thirdParties: The other driver and their insurer
missing: Who is acting for the estate (executor or administrator)
innocent: Gaps in what she knows about the policy and the paperwork are expected from a bereaved relative
questions: Ask gently, once, who will be dealing with his estate and how she would like to be contacted
steps: Give her one named contact and record her needs so she does not have to repeat the story
Accept a copy of the death certificate once, by photo or email, and do not ask again
Arrange a replacement vehicle under the policy if available, or through the other driver’s insurer as she is not at fault
Explain plainly that the total loss settlement will be paid to the estate, and that the injury and dependency claim lies against the other driver’s insurer, where solicitors can help her
Do not cancel the policy or chase the direct debit abruptly; agree the next steps with her
assessment: Genuine, not at fault, and a customer in acute vulnerability. Good handling is about care, clarity and speed, not about investigating.
action: Give her a single contact, a car, and clear next steps for the estate and the claim against the other driver.
outcomes: Replacement car within two days; settlement paid to the estate
Family supported to instruct solicitors for the fatal accident claim

title: Three weeks in hospital, and a no-fault form filed on day 45
type: No-fault benefits application filed after the 30-day notice period
story: Policyholder's car was T-boned at an intersection in the Bronx on 4 March. He was taken to hospital with a fractured pelvis and stayed 22 days, then went to a rehabilitation unit. His application for no-fault (personal injury protection) benefits reached the insurer on 18 April, 45 days after the accident. The adjuster's draft letter denies the application as late under the 30-day written notice rule.
statement: I woke up in the hospital and they told me I'd be there a while. I was on morphine for the first week, I didn't know what day it was. My daughter called the insurance from the hospital in the second week, she said they told her someone would send forms. The forms came to my house, and I wasn't home to see them. I filled them in as soon as I got out of rehab.

accounts.text: Admitted 4 March via the emergency department. Pelvic fracture, surgical fixation on 5 March. Discharged 26 March to an inpatient rehabilitation unit; discharged home on 12 April.
15 March: call from a woman saying she is the insured's daughter, reporting an accident and asking about medical bills. Claim forms mailed to the address on the policy on 16 March.

whatHappened: A genuine accident with a serious injury. He could not give written notice within 30 days because he was in hospital and rehabilitation, and his daughter did give oral notice within 15 days.
damage: Fractured pelvis requiring surgery; 39 days as an inpatient. Car: side damage, claimed separately under collision.
thirdParties: The driver who ran the red light and their insurer
evidence: Insurer phone log of the daughter’s call
missing: Written proof of justification for the late application, if not already supplied
innocent: A hospitalized claimant on strong pain medication cannot reasonably complete forms mailed to his empty home
questions: Ask him to provide a short written explanation for the late filing with the hospital dates
steps: Do not deny for lateness alone: the New York no-fault rules allow late written notice where the claimant gives clear and reasonable justification
Treat the hospital and rehabilitation stays, and the daughter’s call on 15 March, as justification and accept the application
Process the medical and lost-wage benefits within the regulatory time limits
Pursue the other driver’s insurer for property damage and consider subrogation for no-fault benefits paid where the law allows
assessment: Genuine and covered. The 30-day rule was missed for a reason the regulations recognise, and the insurer had oral notice within two weeks. A denial would be wrong and likely overturned.
action: Accept the late application with the justification on file and pay benefits.
outcomes: Application accepted; benefits paid
Draft denial withdrawn after a supervisor review

title: A pickup over the center line, a ditch, and no contact
type: Single-vehicle crash blamed on an unidentified "miss-and-run" driver
story: Policyholder says a pickup truck crossed the center line on a two-lane state road near Zanesville, Ohio, at night, and she swerved into a ditch. There was no contact and the pickup did not stop. She broke her wrist and the car's front end and suspension are damaged. She has claimed under collision for the car and under uninsured motorist coverage for her injury. Ohio law requires independent evidence, beyond her own account, that an unidentified driver caused an injury.
statement: Its headlights were in my lane, right in front of me, I just yanked the wheel. I ended up nose down in the ditch. I called 911 straight away, I was shaking. It was a big pickup, dark color, it kept going. I didn't hit anything except the ditch.

accounts.text: Call from the policyholder at 22:41 reporting a crash into a ditch after a truck came into her lane. A separate call at 22:31 from a commercial driver reports a dark pickup weaving across the center line about 4 miles east, heading west toward the crash location.

Single vehicle off the right side of the road into a ditch. Swerve marks begin in the westbound lane. No debris from another vehicle. Driver states a vehicle crossed the center line. No other vehicle located.

whatHappened: Probably a genuine evasive swerve caused by an unidentified driver; the earlier 911 call about a weaving pickup may provide the independent corroboration her injury claim needs.
damage: Her Malibu: front bumper, radiator, front suspension, estimate $6,200. Fractured right wrist.
thirdParties: The commercial driver who made the earlier 911 call
evidence: Deputy's crash report with swerve marks
Hospital record of the wrist fracture
missing: A statement from the commercial driver who called at 22:31
Any camera at the gas station a mile east
indicators: No contact and no independent witness at the crash itself
innocent: Miss-and-run crashes are real and often leave only swerve marks
The earlier 911 call fits the time and direction
questions: Ask the sheriff’s office for the commercial driver’s contact details
Ask her whether she was tired or on her phone
steps: Pay the car under collision, subject to the deductible: collision does not depend on another driver
For the uninsured motorist injury claim, look for independent corroborative evidence: her own account is not enough under Ohio law, but the earlier 911 call and swerve marks may be
Interview the commercial driver who called at 22:31
Decide the UM claim on the corroboration found, and explain the requirement to her plainly
assessment: Insufficient evidence for now, not suspicion. Collision cover applies to the car. The injury claim turns on independent corroboration, and a promising lead exists in the earlier 911 call.
action: Pay collision, trace the earlier caller and decide the uninsured motorist claim on the corroboration.
outcomes: Commercial driver confirms the weaving pickup; UM claim paid
Caller cannot be traced; UM claim declined with an explanation of the corroboration rule

title: He chose $250,000 of PIP, and the bills will pass a million
type: Catastrophic injury on a Michigan policy with a limited PIP medical choice
story: Policyholder's pickup was hit at an intersection in Grand Rapids by a driver who slid through a red light on ice. He suffered a spinal cord injury. At renewal in 2023 he signed a form choosing a $250,000 limit for personal injury protection medical benefits instead of unlimited cover. His rehabilitation team estimates lifetime medical and care costs well above $1 million. His wife has asked to be paid for caring for him at home.

title: Limited tort, eight physical therapy sessions, and a demand for pain and suffering

title: The roommate took the keys from the bowl

Ask whether the roommate has his own insurance

Check his own auto policy, which may respond either way

Use found to exceed any permission; third parties referred to his own insurer

title: A Tacoma valued with comparables 300 miles away

title: Aftermarket headlamps in front of the radar

accounts.text: Vendor: Mile High Auto Rentals. Created by user ID of the handling adjuster. Tax ID not verified. Address: a mailbox store. Bank account added the same day. 23 payments totalling $31,870 on 19 claims, all assigned to the same adjuster.
Rental paid by the policyholder's card: 14 days, $1,260. Rental company is a national chain, not Mile High Auto Rentals.

whatHappened: The customer's claim is genuine. Her reimbursement was diverted to a fictitious vendor controlled by the adjuster, who appears to have done the same on other claims.
damage: Customer unpaid $1,260. Possible insider loss of $31,870 across 19 claims.
evidence: Payment history for the vendor account
missing: Bank records for the vendor account
Whether other customers on the 19 claims were paid
inconsistencies: Payment recorded to a rental company she never used
indicators: Vendor created by the same person who approves its payments
Unverified tax ID and a mailbox address
Payments concentrated on one adjuster’s claims
innocent: Data entry errors can misdirect a single payment, but not 23 payments to an unverified vendor
questions: Check every one of the 19 claims for customers who were not paid
steps: Pay the customer her $1,260 now and apologize: she is not part of the problem
Refer to the special investigations unit and internal audit, preserve the system records, and restrict the adjuster’s access pending investigation
Contact every customer on the affected claims and pay anyone who was not paid
Fix the control gap: no user should be able to create a vendor and approve payments to it
Report as required to the state fraud bureau and law enforcement
assessment: The claim is genuine; the fraud is internal. The priority is to make the customer whole, then contain and investigate the insider scheme.
action: Pay the customer, escalate to investigations and audit, and close the control gap.
outcomes: Adjuster dismissed and charged; all affected customers paid
Vendor controls changed to require independent approval

title: Stolen from the mall on the 12th, on a ship since the 25th of last month
type: Theft claim for a car already exported
story: Policyholder reported his 2022 Lexus RX stolen from a mall parking lot in Newark, New Jersey, on 12 September. He produced both keys. A routine export check of the VIN shows the vehicle was declared for export and loaded into a container at Port Newark on 25 August, eighteen days before the reported theft. The vehicle is financed and he made his 1 September loan payment.
statement: I parked by the food court and went in for an hour. When I came out it was gone. I've got both keys right here. I don't know anything about any export, maybe someone cloned my VIN. I need the money to pay off the loan.

accounts.text: VIN matches a used vehicle export declaration filed 22 August. Container loaded at Port Newark on 25 August. Exporter: a freight forwarder in Elizabeth, NJ. Title copy submitted with the declaration in the policyholder's name.
No camera coverage of the stated parking row. Entrance camera footage for 12 September reviewed for the plate: no match found entering the lot.

whatHappened: The car was exported with a copy of his title before he reported it stolen. The theft report is false.
damage: Claimed total loss $52,000. No damage; vehicle overseas.
missing: The freight forwarder’s booking records and who paid them
inconsistencies: Reported stolen on 12 September; exported on 25 August
Entrance cameras show no sign of the car entering the lot
indicators: Export with his title copy before the reported theft
Both keys produced
Financed vehicle
innocent: VIN cloning exists, but a declaration with his own title copy makes it very unlikely
questions: Ask the freight forwarder who booked and paid for the export
Ask the policyholder to explain how a copy of his title was used
steps: Refer to the special investigations unit and to the National Insurance Crime Bureau
Get the freight forwarder’s records through the proper legal process
Take an examination under oath under the policy if the facts are disputed
Deny the claim on the evidence and report to the state fraud bureau as required
assessment: Confirmed fraud: the car was exported with his title copy 18 days before he reported it stolen.
action: Deny, refer to the special investigations unit and NICB, and report to the state.
outcomes: Claim withdrawn after the forwarder names him as the customer; prosecuted
Denied after the examination under oath

title: Fifty-two days and no decision, in California
type: Claim handling outside California’s regulatory time limits
story: Policyholder reported a collision claim on 2 June after her car was sideswiped in a San Jose parking structure. She sent photos, the repair estimate and the other driver's details on 10 June. The adjuster went on leave. Nobody acknowledged the claim until 21 June, and on 1 August, 52 days after her proof of claim, there is still no decision and no letter explaining what is needed. She has filed a complaint with the Department of Insurance.
statement: I sent everything you asked for in the first week. I've called nine times and left messages. Nobody told me anything was missing. I'm paying for a rental out of my own pocket. I've complained to the state because I didn't know what else to do.

accounts.text: 2 June: first notice. 10 June: proof of claim received (estimate, photos, other party details). 21 June: acknowledgment sent. No further written communication. Nine inbound calls logged, no return calls. Adjuster on leave from 8 June; file not reassigned.
Consumer complaint received regarding delay in claim handling. Please provide a full response and copies of all correspondence.

whatHappened: A straightforward claim left unattended when the adjuster went on leave, breaching California's time limits for acknowledging, deciding and communicating.
damage: Her Corolla: driver's side doors, estimate $2,950. Rental costs paid by her.
thirdParties: The other driver and their insurer
missing: Any reason the file was not reassigned during the leave
innocent: An unplanned leave without a handover can leave a file invisible to the rest of the team
questions: Check whether other files of the same adjuster were left unassigned
steps: Decide the claim now and pay within the time allowed after acceptance
Recognise the breaches: acknowledgment is due within 15 calendar days of notice, and acceptance or denial within 40 days of proof of claim, with written notice every 30 days if more time is needed
Respond fully and promptly to the Department of Insurance with the file history
Reimburse her reasonable rental costs caused by the delay and apologize
Reassign the adjuster’s other files and fix the leave cover process
assessment: Genuine claim, clear regulatory breaches by the insurer. The fix is to pay, answer the regulator candidly and stop it recurring.
action: Pay the claim and rental costs, respond to the Department of Insurance, and review the leave cover process.
outcomes: Claim paid in 3 days; complaint closed with a finding against the insurer
Audit finds 14 other files of the same adjuster overdue

title: The claim file that went to the other Michael Brown
type: Claim documents with personal data emailed to the wrong claimant
story: An adjuster in Boston emailed the injury claim file of policyholder Michael J. Brown to a different claimant, Michael R. Brown, because the email address auto-completed. The attachment included his driver's license image, medical records and a medical bill showing his Social Security number. The recipient replied an hour later: "I think this isn't mine." The adjuster has not told anyone.
statement: I was rear-ended in March and I've been through enough. Now you're telling me a stranger has my medical records and my Social Security number? What are you going to do about it?

accounts.text: Sent 14:06 to michael.r.brown@ (another claimant's address) instead of michael.j.brown@. Attachment: claim file PDF, 41 pages, not encrypted. Reply received 15:02: "I think this isn't mine, I haven't opened most of it."
Driver's license image; hospital and physical therapy records; a medical bill showing the full Social Security number; claim notes.

whatHappened: A genuine claim, and a privacy incident caused by an auto-completed email address. Sensitive personal information went to an unintended recipient.
damage: Exposure of driver's license, medical records and Social Security number. No financial loss known yet.
thirdParties: Michael R. Brown, the unintended recipient
missing: Written confirmation from the recipient that the email and attachment are deleted
innocent: Auto-complete errors are a common cause of misdirected email
questions: Ask the recipient to confirm in writing that he has deleted the email and any copies
steps: Report the incident to the privacy or compliance team today, as company policy requires
Contain it: ask the recipient to delete the email and confirm in writing
Assess notification duties under the state breach notification and insurance data security laws: a Social Security number and medical records are sensitive data
Notify the policyholder, offer credit monitoring, and notify regulators if the law requires
Fix the cause: send sensitive files only through a secure portal, and turn off auto-complete for external addresses
assessment: The injury claim is genuine; the incident is the insurer's. Sensitive data was exposed, so containment, assessment and likely notification are needed promptly.
action: Escalate to the privacy team, contain the disclosure, notify the policyholder with support, and assess regulatory notification.
outcomes: Recipient confirms deletion; policyholder notified with credit monitoring; regulator notified
