Secure portal made mandatory for medical records

title: A recorded statement in English, and a customer who speaks Spanish
type: Fault decided from a statement taken without an interpreter
story: Policyholder, whose first language is Spanish, gave a recorded statement in English two days after a collision at a stop sign in San Antonio. In it she answers "yes" to the question "So you didn't stop at the sign?" The adjuster assigned her 100% fault. Her daughter has called to say her mother did not understand the questions and did stop. A neighbour's doorbell camera has since been found.
statement: (Through her daughter, translated) I stopped at the sign. I always stop there, my grandchildren's school is on that street. The man on the phone talked very fast. I said yes because I thought he was asking if I was okay. Nobody asked me if I wanted Spanish.

accounts.text: Adjuster: "So you didn't stop at the sign?" Insured: "Yes." Adjuster: "Okay, and the other car had the right of way?" Insured: "Yes, yes, okay." No interpreter offered. Duration 6 minutes.
Her car slows to a near stop at the line, then pulls forward. The other car enters the frame at speed from the right, without slowing, about 1.5 seconds before impact.

whatHappened: She did essentially stop. Her "yes" answers came from a language misunderstanding, and the fault decision rested on them.
damage: Her Altima: front-right corner, $3,600. Other car: driver's side.
thirdParties: The other driver and their insurer
missing: The other driver's speed
A statement from her taken with a qualified interpreter
inconsistencies: The transcript records her agreeing she did not stop; the camera shows she slowed to a near stop
innocent: People answering in a second language often say yes to show they are listening
questions: Retake her statement in Spanish with a qualified interpreter
Ask the other driver about his speed
steps: Do not rely on the English statement: it was taken without checking her language needs
Retake the statement with a qualified interpreter, and record her language preference on the file
Re-decide fault on the camera footage and the new statement; the other driver’s speed may make fault shared or his
Apologize, explain the review, and correct any fault record or premium effect
assessment: Disputed, but the fault decision is unsafe: it rests on a statement she did not understand, and the independent camera contradicts it.
action: Retake the statement with an interpreter, reopen the fault decision on the camera evidence, and correct the record.
outcomes: Fault changed to 50/50 after review; record corrected
Other driver found mainly at fault for speeding; recovery made

title: Told the agent on WhatsApp the same day, registered 38 days later
type: Own-damage claim intimated to the agent but never registered with the insurer
story: Policyholder's car was scraped along its side by a private bus at a junction in Visakhapatnam. That evening he sent photos and a message to his insurance agent on WhatsApp, and the agent replied "noted sir, will register". No claim was registered. Thirty-eight days later he called the insurer's toll-free number to ask about the survey and was told his claim was being treated as intimated late. The car has not been repaired.
statement: I have always gone through my agent, he sold me the policy and he handles everything. He said he would register it. I waited for the surveyor to call. When nobody came I phoned the company myself. The car is standing in my parking exactly as it was, nothing has been touched.

accounts.text: Accident day, 19:42: four photos of the damage and "Sir bus scraped my car at Siripuram junction, please register claim". 19:58, agent: "noted sir, will register". No further messages for five weeks.
Claim registered 38 days after the accident date via the call centre. Remark: late intimation, refer to claims manager. Agent code linked to the policy.

whatHappened: A genuine accident that the policyholder reported to the insurer's own agent the same evening. The agent failed to register it.
damage: Hyundai i20: left doors, rear quarter panel and mirror scraped and dented; estimate ₹46,000. Unrepaired.
evidence: WhatsApp messages with time stamps and photos
missing: The bus registration number and its operator's insurer
innocent: Many policyholders treat their agent as the insurer and rely on the agent to register claims
questions: Ask the agent why the claim was not registered
Ask whether he noted the bus number
steps: Treat the date of the WhatsApp message to the agent as the date of intimation: the agent acts for the insurer and the delay is not the policyholder’s
Arrange a survey now; the car is unrepaired, so nothing has been lost by the delay
Settle on merit within the regulator’s timelines once the survey report is in
Take up the agent’s failure with the agency team
assessment: Genuine claim, intimated in time to the insurer's agent. The delay causes no prejudice and should not be held against him.
action: Condone the delay, survey and settle, and address the agent's lapse.
outcomes: Survey done next day; claim settled
Agent counselled and the WhatsApp channel added to the claims intake process

title: A road test by the service centre, and a motorcyclist in hospital
type: Accident while the car was being driven by a dealer’s technician during servicing
story: Policyholder left her car at an authorised service centre in Chennai for a noise in the suspension. During the afternoon the car hit a motorcyclist on Anna Salai, who suffered a fractured leg. The service centre says the policyholder's son was driving with a technician beside him. The job card and the gate register show the car went out on a "road test" with a technician. The rider's family has filed a claim before the tribunal against the owner and the insurer.
statement: I dropped the car at 9 in the morning and went to work. My son was in college all day, he has an exam this week. Nobody from my family drove that car. The service centre called me at 4 and said there was a small accident on the test drive.

accounts.text: Job card: "Customer complaint: noise from front suspension. Road test by technician before and after work." Gate register: out 14:10, driver name of a service centre technician, purpose "road test"; in 15:35.
The customer's son came to check the car and asked to drive it on the road test. Our technician was in the passenger seat. The customer's policy should cover it, it is her car.

whatHappened: The car was being driven on a road test by the service centre in connection with its trade. Who was at the wheel is disputed, but the use was the service centre's.
damage: Motorcyclist: fractured tibia, surgery. Policyholder's car: front bumper and bonnet, ₹38,000. Motorcycle: front fork and wheel.
thirdParties: The authorised service centre and its motor trade insurer
missing: The son's college attendance record for that afternoon
CCTV from the service centre gate
The service centre’s motor trade policy
inconsistencies: The manager says the son drove; the gate register names the technician as driver
The policyholder says her son was in college all day
innocent: A manager may genuinely believe a family member was present if someone came to collect paperwork
questions: Ask the college for the son’s attendance that afternoon
Ask the service centre for its gate CCTV and its motor trade policy
steps: Establish who drove from the gate register, CCTV and the son’s attendance record

Note that the standard private car policy excludes use for any purpose in connection with the motor trade; a road test during servicing is such a use, so the service centre’s motor trade policy should respond
Defend the tribunal claim on that basis, but if the tribunal makes the owner’s insurer satisfy the award, seek recovery from the service centre and its insurer
Settle the owner’s own damage through the service centre, which had custody of the car
assessment: Disputed on who drove, but the documents point to the technician. The use was the service centre's, so primary responsibility lies with its motor trade cover.
action: Gather the gate CCTV and attendance record, put the service centre's insurer on notice, and protect the injured rider's claim while liability is sorted out.
outcomes: Tribunal holds the service centre’s insurer liable; owner’s insurer released
Award paid by the owner’s insurer and recovered from the service centre

title: He opted out of the ₹15 lakh cover because he had another one
type: Owner-driver death where compulsory personal accident cover was opted out
story: Policyholder, aged 52, died when a lorry ran into the back of his scooter on the outer ring road in Mysuru. His widow has claimed the ₹15 lakh owner-driver personal accident cover under the scooter's policy. The policy shows he opted out of that cover at purchase, declaring that he held a separate personal accident policy of ₹15 lakh. That separate policy lapsed two months before the accident and was not renewed.
statement: My husband always took insurance seriously. He said he had a bigger accident policy from his office so he didn't need it twice. I didn't know the other one had stopped. Now I have two children in college. The lorry driver ran away but the police found the lorry.

accounts.text: Two-wheeler package policy. Compulsory personal accident cover for owner-driver: not opted. Declaration signed by the insured: "I hold a general personal accident policy with a sum insured of ₹15 lakh or more."
Lorry hit the scooter from behind at about 22:00. Driver fled; lorry traced the next day and seized. Case registered against the lorry driver for rash and negligent driving causing death.

whatHappened: He opted out of the owner-driver personal accident cover in good faith, relying on a policy that later lapsed. The motor policy has no personal accident cover to pay.
damage: Death of the owner-driver. Scooter damaged beyond repair.
evidence: Policy schedule with the opt-out declaration
Lapse notice of the separate PA policy
missing: Whether the employer’s group personal accident cover still applied
The lorry’s insurance details
innocent: Many owners opt out because they believe an employer cover protects them
questions: Ask the family whether his employer had any group accident cover in force
Get the lorry’s insurance details from the police
steps: Explain kindly that the scooter’s policy does not include the owner-driver personal accident cover because he opted out
Pay the own-damage claim for the scooter under the package policy
Help the family check any employer group cover, and explain their right to claim compensation from the lorry’s insurer before the motor accident claims tribunal
Check that the opt-out declaration was properly taken at sale
assessment: Genuine and tragic, but the personal accident benefit was not bought. The family's main remedy is the claim against the lorry's insurer.
action: Decline the personal accident benefit with care, pay the scooter, and guide the family to the tribunal claim and any employer cover.
outcomes: Family receives compensation through the tribunal claim against the lorry’s insurer
Employer group cover found and paid

title: Wedding guests in the back of a Tata Ace
type: Goods vehicle carrying passengers overturns, with deaths and injuries
story: A Tata Ace mini truck insured as a goods carriage was carrying nine wedding guests in its cargo area when it overturned on a bend near Bhilwara, Rajasthan. Two passengers died and six were injured. The families have filed claims before the motor accident claims tribunal against the owner and the insurer. The policy covers liability to third parties and to the owner of the goods travelling with them, not to passengers carried free of charge.
statement: It was my cousin's wedding and the jeep we booked didn't come. Everyone asked me to take them to the village in my Ace. I said it isn't for people but they insisted. The road bent suddenly and the back swung out. I will never forgive myself.

accounts.text: Goods vehicle carrying 9 persons in the cargo body and 2 in the cabin overturned on a curve. Two deaths at the spot, six injured. Driver-owner holds a valid licence for the vehicle class. No goods on board.

Goods carrying commercial vehicle, liability only plus own damage. Limitations as to use: carriage of goods. Persons covered beyond third parties: owner of goods or their representative travelling in the vehicle. No cover for other passengers.

whatHappened: The owner-driver used a goods vehicle to carry passengers free of charge, in breach of the policy, and lost control on a bend.
damage: Two deaths and six injured passengers. Tata Ace overturned, cabin and body damaged.
thirdParties: Families of the two deceased passengers
evidence: Policy schedule and limitations as to use
missing: Post-mortem reports and medical records for the injured
Whether any passenger paid a fare
innocent: In rural areas goods vehicles are often pressed into service when booked transport fails
questions: Confirm whether anyone paid to travel, which would change the analysis to hire or reward
steps: Defend the claims on the policy breach: the policy does not cover gratuitous passengers in a goods vehicle
Expect the tribunal may still direct the insurer to satisfy the awards first and recover the amount from the owner; plan for that recovery
Decline the own-damage claim for use outside the permitted purpose
Treat the families with care in all communication; they are victims, not the policyholder
assessment: Genuine tragedy caused by an unlawful use of a goods vehicle. The insurer has a strong policy defence against the passenger claims, but may have to pay first and recover from the owner.
action: Contest liability on the breach, prepare for any order to pay first, and pursue recovery from the owner.
outcomes: Tribunal orders the insurer to pay the awards and recover from the owner
Insurer exonerated; awards fall on the owner

title: A driving licence that Sarathi has never heard of
type: Truck accident where the employed driver’s licence was fake
story: A truck belonging to a transport company in Nagpur ran into the back of a car in fog on the Nagpur–Amravati highway, injuring two occupants. The truck's driver had worked for the company for 14 months. After the accident the licence he had produced turned out not to exist on the Sarathi licence database. The company says it inspected his licence card, made him take a driving test and checked his previous employer before hiring him.
statement: We have thirty trucks and we check every driver. He showed us his card, he drove for an hour with our senior driver, and his old employer said he was good. He had no accidents in fourteen months. How are we supposed to know a card is fake when it looks real?

accounts.text: Licence number produced by the driver: no record found. No licence of any class issued in the driver's name in the state shown on the card.
Copy of the licence card. Driving test report signed by the senior driver, rated good. Reference call note from the previous employer. Appointment letter 14 months before the accident.

whatHappened: The driver deceived his employer with a fake licence. The company took reasonable care in hiring him but did not verify the licence online.
damage: Car occupants: one fracture, one soft-tissue injury. Car: rear end, ₹2,10,000. Truck: front bumper and grille.
missing: Whether the company could have verified the licence online at the time of hiring
indicators: Licence with no record on the national database
innocent: A good-quality fake card can deceive an employer who checks the card and tests the driver
questions: Ask the company whether it had any process to verify licences online
steps: Satisfy the third-party claims: the insurer can only avoid liability against the owner if it proves the owner failed to take reasonable care over the licence, which the hiring file makes hard
Decide the truck’s own damage with legal advice: the driver clause is breached on its face, but the owner’s due diligence weighs against repudiation
Report the fake licence to the police
Advise the company to verify all licences on the national database
assessment: Genuine accident; the owner is a victim of the driver's deception and took reasonable care. Third-party liability stands; avoiding cover against the owner would be hard to justify.
action: Pay the third parties, take a reasoned decision on own damage, and report the fake licence.
outcomes: Third parties paid; own damage paid after legal review
Tribunal refuses the insurer’s plea to be exonerated

title: The surveyor recommends repudiation because the PUC had expired
type: Own-damage claim queried because the pollution certificate had lapsed
story: Policyholder's car was rear-ended by a tempo at a signal in Pune in the rain. She has claimed for the repairs under her own policy. The surveyor's report confirms the damage is consistent with the accident and assesses it at ₹54,000, but adds: "PUC certificate expired three months before the accident. Recommend repudiation." She renewed the PUC the day after the accident.
statement: The PUC slipped my mind, I'm usually careful. I got it done the next day and the car passed easily. I don't see what pollution has to do with a tempo hitting me from behind. The tempo driver admitted it.

accounts.text: Damage to rear bumper, boot lid and tail lamps consistent with a rear impact. Assessed loss ₹54,000. Driving licence and registration valid. PUC certificate expired three months before the accident. Recommend repudiation.
The road was wet and my brakes didn't hold. I hit her car from behind. I gave her my owner's number.

whatHappened: A genuine rear-end collision. The lapsed pollution certificate has nothing to do with the loss and is not a ground to deny the claim.
damage: Honda City: rear bumper, boot lid and tail lamps, assessed ₹54,000.
evidence: New PUC certificate issued the next day
missing: The tempo's insurance details
innocent: Pollution certificates are easy to let lapse
questions: Ask for the tempo owner's details for recovery
steps: Do not repudiate: IRDAI clarified in August 2020 that not holding a valid PUC certificate is not a valid reason to deny a motor claim
Settle the assessed loss within seven days of the survey report
Remind her that a valid PUC is needed at renewal and is a legal requirement for driving
Correct the surveyor’s recommendation in the file
assessment: Genuine and payable. The PUC lapse is a traffic offence, not a policy ground for refusal.
action: Settle ₹54,000 less any excess, and correct the repudiation recommendation.
outcomes: Claim settled within a week
Surveyor’s report template updated

title: Depreciation at 40% on a car that was four and a half years old
type: Depreciation applied at the wrong rates in a partial loss assessment
story: Policyholder's SUV hit a road divider in Lucknow after swerving for a stray dog. It was first registered on 11 March 2021 and the accident happened on 2 October 2025. His policy has no zero-depreciation add-on. The settlement letter deducts depreciation of 40% on metal parts, 50% on plastic parts, 50% on the windscreen and 50% on paint materials. He says the deductions are too high.
statement: I know I don't have zero dep, the agent explained that. But 40% on the bonnet and 50% on the windscreen? My car isn't even five years old. A friend at another company says glass has no depreciation at all.

accounts.text: Bonnet, front fender (metal): depreciation 40%. Front bumper (plastic): 50%. Windscreen (glass): 50%. Paint materials: 50%. Labour: nil. Vehicle age taken as "5 years".
Date of first registration: 11 March 2021.

whatHappened: A genuine accident. The assessment used the wrong vehicle age for metal parts and wrongly depreciated the glass.
damage: Creta: bonnet, front fender, front bumper and windscreen. Metal parts ₹64,000, plastic ₹18,000, windscreen ₹14,000, paint materials ₹9,000, labour ₹16,000.
missing: The surveyor’s working for the vehicle age
inconsistencies: The sheet takes the age as 5 years; the car was 4 years and about 7 months old
innocent: Rounding the age up is a common error in assessment sheets
questions: Ask the surveyor to recompute the age from the date of first registration
steps: Recompute the age: 4 years and about 7 months, so metal parts take 35% depreciation, not 40%
Apply nil depreciation to glass parts, 50% to plastic and rubber parts, and 50% to paint materials only
Pay the difference with a revised assessment sheet that shows each rate
Check for the same error in the surveyor’s other assessments
assessment: Genuine claim, wrongly assessed. Under the standard depreciation schedule metal parts at this age take 35% and glass takes none.
action: Revise the assessment at the correct rates and pay the difference.
outcomes: Revised settlement adds about ₹10,200
Complaint closed after the revised sheet is sent

title: An auto worth ₹1.2 lakh, a repair bill of ₹96,000, and a family that needs it back
type: Auto-rickshaw near the constructive total loss threshold
story: Policyholder's CNG auto-rickshaw was hit on its side by a private bus in heavy rain in Chennai. Its insured declared value is ₹1,20,000. The surveyor assessed repairs at ₹96,000, which is 80% of the insured value, and proposed treating it as a constructive total loss. The owner wants it repaired. A week later his garage sent a revised estimate of ₹88,000, replacing new parts with refurbished ones.
statement: This auto feeds my family. If you take it away, getting a new one and the permit sorted will take months. My garage can fix it. I asked them to bring the estimate down so you would allow the repair. I just want to get back on the road.

accounts.text: Chassis bent on the left side, body shell and roof frame damaged, CNG cylinder mounting distorted. Repair cost ₹96,000 against IDV ₹1,20,000: exceeds 75%. Recommend constructive total loss.
Chassis straightening instead of replacement. Refurbished roof frame and refurbished CNG cylinder bracket. Total ₹88,000.

whatHappened: A genuine accident that pushes the repair cost past 75% of the insured value. The lower estimate was produced to avoid a total loss, partly with refurbished safety-related parts.
damage: Auto-rickshaw: chassis, body shell, roof frame and CNG cylinder mounting damaged.
thirdParties: The private bus operator and its insurer
missing: The bus operator's insurance details for recovery
inconsistencies: The revised estimate cuts the cost by using refurbished parts, including a CNG cylinder bracket
innocent: An owner desperate to keep his livelihood will naturally push for a cheaper repair
questions: Ask the owner whether he would accept a settlement that lets him keep the vehicle and repair it himself
steps: Do not accept the refurbished CNG cylinder bracket or a straightened chassis without an engineer’s approval: they are safety-critical on a CNG vehicle
Treat it as a constructive total loss on the surveyor’s figures, since repair exceeds 75% of the insured value
Offer a settlement on a net-of-salvage basis so he keeps the vehicle and can repair it at his own garage
Explain the options plainly and settle quickly; pursue the bus operator’s insurer
assessment: Genuine claim; a constructive total loss. A net-of-salvage settlement meets his need to keep the auto without accepting an unsafe estimate.
action: Settle as a total loss net of salvage, let him keep and repair the vehicle, and recover from the bus operator.
outcomes: Settled net of salvage; auto repaired and back on the road in three weeks
Owner chooses the full IDV and buys a new auto

title: Halfway through a cashless repair, the garage was delisted
type: Cashless repair interrupted when the network garage was removed from the network
story: Policyholder's car was taken to a network garage in Bengaluru after a collision at a junction. The insurer approved a cashless repair of ₹1,42,000 after the survey. Midway through the repair the insurer delisted the garage over billing disputes on other claims. The garage now says it will not release the car unless she pays the full ₹1,42,000 herself and claims it back.
statement: Your company sent me to that garage and approved the repair. Now I'm told it's not your garage any more and I have to pay one lakh forty-two thousand to get my own car back. I don't have that kind of money lying around. I've been taking autos to work for three weeks.

accounts.text: Cashless approval for ₹1,42,000 issued 9 days after the accident, subject to final bill and re-inspection. Garage status at approval: network.
Garage delisted with immediate effect from 16 days after the accident. Instruction: no new cashless claims. No instruction on claims already approved.

whatHappened: A genuine claim caught by the insurer's own delisting decision. The repair was approved while the garage was in the network.
damage: Baleno: front end, radiator and airbag module. Approved repair ₹1,42,000.
missing: Re-inspection of the completed repair
innocent: The garage is protecting itself after losing its network status; holding the car is leverage, not evidence of wrongdoing on this claim
questions: Ask the garage how much of the approved work is complete
steps: Honour the cashless approval for the work already authorised: it was given while the garage was in the network, and the delisting was the insurer’s decision
Re-inspect, then pay the garage directly against the final bill so the car is released without her paying
If the garage refuses, settle her reimbursement within seven days of receiving the documents
Fix the delisting process so approved claims are handled before a garage is removed
assessment: Genuine claim; the problem was created by the insurer. The customer should not have to fund the repair.
action: Pay the garage directly under the existing approval and get the car released.
outcomes: Car released within two days after direct payment
Process changed so approved claims are completed before delisting

title: One key for the stolen Scorpio, and a duplicate cut three weeks earlier
type: Theft claim where only one key is produced and a duplicate key was recently made
story: Policyholder reported his Mahindra Scorpio stolen from outside his house in Rohini, Delhi, overnight. An FIR was registered the next morning and the insurer was informed the same day. For settlement he has produced one key and says the second was lost two years ago on a trek in Himachal. The authorised dealer's records show a duplicate key was cut at his request three weeks before the theft.
statement: The second key fell in a river near Kasol two years ago, my friends were there. I don't remember any duplicate key. Maybe the dealer has the wrong car. The police say these Scorpios are stolen to order.

accounts.text: Duplicate key programmed 23 days before the theft. Request in the customer's name, paid in cash. Vehicle brought in by a person signing as "driver".
FIR registered for theft of the vehicle. Investigation ongoing; vehicle not traced. Final report not yet filed.

whatHappened: The theft may be genuine, but a duplicate key cut three weeks before, which he does not mention, needs explaining before settlement.
damage: Scorpio stolen; IDV ₹11,80,000.
thirdParties: The person who brought the car in for the duplicate key
missing: The duplicate key
Who the "driver" was
Dealer CCTV of the day the key was cut
The non-traceable report from the police and court
inconsistencies: He says he knows nothing of a duplicate key; the dealer cut one at his request three weeks before
indicators: Duplicate key made shortly before the theft
Only one key produced
Cash payment by an unnamed driver
innocent: A driver or family member may have ordered the key without telling him
Thieves sometimes obtain keys by deception at dealers
questions: Ask whether he employs a driver and who took the car to the dealer
Ask the dealer for CCTV and the signature on the request
steps: Put the dealer record to him and take a written explanation
Investigate the duplicate key with the dealer’s CCTV and the signature
Do not settle until the explanation is checked and the non-traceable report is received; then decide on merit
Collect the remaining settlement documents in parallel: the RC, the remaining key, transfer forms and subrogation letter
assessment: Suspicious, not proven. The undisclosed duplicate key is the central question; it may have an innocent answer through a driver.
action: Investigate the duplicate key before settlement and keep the theft paperwork moving.
outcomes: Driver admits ordering the key and is arrested with a gang; claim paid
Claim repudiated after CCTV shows the policyholder at the dealer

title: Loan closed in March, bank still on the RC in October
type: Total loss settlement where the hypothecation was never removed
story: Policyholder's car was declared a total loss after a head-on collision on a highway near Jaipur. The registration certificate still shows hypothecation to a co-operative bank. She repaid the loan in March and has the bank's no-objection certificate and a zero-dues letter, but never had the hypothecation removed at the RTO. The settlement team says it can only pay the bank.
statement: I finished paying in March, I have the letters. The bank says it has no claim on my car. Why should the money go to them and come back to me in a few weeks? I need it to put down on another car.

accounts.text: No-objection certificate for termination of hypothecation, dated in March, with Form 35 signed by the bank. Separate letter confirming the loan account is closed with no dues.
Hypothecated to the co-operative bank. No termination endorsed.

whatHappened: A genuine total loss where the loan is paid off but the hypothecation entry was never removed.
damage: Car total loss; IDV ₹6,40,000.
missing: Confirmation from the bank direct, not only through the customer
innocent: Many owners never get round to removing hypothecation after closing a loan
questions: Confirm with the bank directly that the loan is closed
steps: Verify the NOC and zero-dues letter with the bank directly
Once verified, pay the settlement to her, with the bank’s written consent on file
Collect the transfer documents for the salvage, including the bank’s Form 35
Explain the timeline to her so she can plan the new purchase
assessment: Genuine and straightforward once the bank confirms. Paying the bank would add delay for no purpose.
action: Verify with the bank and pay her directly.
outcomes: Bank confirms; settlement paid to her within a week
Bank insists on joint cheque; paid jointly and released the same day

title: Treated free under the scheme, then billed to us as well
type: Hospital bill for a road accident victim already treated under the cashless scheme
story: Our policyholder's car hit a pedestrian, Mr Patil, on a road in Nashik. He was taken to a designated hospital and treated for six days under the government's cashless treatment scheme for road accident victims. The hospital has now sent our claims team a bill of ₹1,52,000 for "direct settlement" of the same admission. Mr Patil's lawyer has also included the same hospital bills in his claim before the motor accident claims tribunal.
statement: (Lawyer for Mr Patil) My client suffered a fractured femur and was in hospital for six days. The hospital bills are part of his medical expenses and are claimed in full from the insurer of the vehicle, along with his loss of earnings and pain and suffering.

accounts.text: Victim admitted under the Cashless Treatment of Road Accident Victims Scheme, 2025. Treatment package approved and paid to the hospital: ₹1,38,000 for six days from the date of the accident. Status: settled by the State Health Agency.

accounts.who: Hospital bill sent to the insurer
accounts.text: Inpatient bill for the same admission dates: ₹1,52,000. Request: direct settlement by the insurer of the offending vehicle. No mention of the scheme payment.

whatHappened: The hospital was paid for this treatment under the scheme and has billed the insurer again for the same admission. The lawyer has probably included the bills without knowing the scheme paid them.
damage: Pedestrian: fractured femur, six days in hospital, about three months off work.
evidence: Hospital bill sent to the insurer
missing: Any treatment after the seven days the scheme covers
Proof of his earnings
inconsistencies: The hospital was paid ₹1,38,000 by the scheme for the same admission it now bills at ₹1,52,000
indicators: Same admission billed twice
No mention of the scheme payment in the bill
innocent: Hospital billing teams may not link scheme payments to later insurer requests
Lawyers often claim all bills given to them by the family
questions: Ask the hospital to explain the bill against the scheme payment
Ask the lawyer for any treatment costs after the scheme period
steps: Do not pay the hospital’s bill: the admission was already paid under the scheme
In the tribunal claim, ask that medical expenses met by the scheme be excluded, so compensation is not paid twice
Report the duplicate bill to the State Health Agency
Handle the rest of the claim on merit: loss of earnings, pain and suffering and any later treatment
assessment: The injury claim is genuine; the medical bill is a duplicate. The hospital's request is suspicious, not proven fraud, and the lawyer's inclusion is probably an error.
action: Refuse the duplicate bill, exclude scheme-paid expenses in the tribunal claim, and settle the remaining heads on evidence.
outcomes: Hospital withdraws its bill; claim settled without the duplicate expenses
State Health Agency investigates the hospital’s billing

title: Five lakh without proving fault, or more if they can
type: Death claim where the family must choose between no-fault and fault-based compensation
story: Our policyholder's truck hit and killed Raju Yadav, aged 32, a construction worker, as he crossed a road on the outskirts of Patna in fog at dawn. His widow filed a claim for the fixed no-fault compensation of ₹5 lakh under section 164 of the Motor Vehicles Act. Her lawyer now says she will also file a fault-based claim under section 166 for loss of dependency, which could be several times larger.
statement: He earned about fifteen thousand a month on the sites and sent everything home. We have two small children and his mother. People told me to file the five lakh first because it is quick. Now the lawyer says we can get more. I don't understand which one we should do.

accounts.text: Pedestrian struck by a truck in dense fog at about 05:40 while crossing the road. Driver states he could not see. Truck speed not established. No pedestrian crossing nearby. Case registered for causing death by negligence.
Claim for fixed compensation of ₹5,00,000 for death, without pleading fault. Filed by the widow on behalf of the dependants.

whatHappened: A genuine fatal accident. The family has started a no-fault claim and is weighing a larger fault-based claim; the law does not allow full compensation under both for the same death.
damage: Death of a 32-year-old earner with four dependants.
missing: Proof of his earnings
Evidence of the truck’s speed and lights in the fog
innocent: Families often file the quick no-fault claim first on advice from others, before understanding the alternative
questions: Ask the lawyer which remedy the family will pursue
steps: Explain, through the designated officer, that section 164 gives fixed compensation without proving fault, and that the family cannot also receive full fault-based compensation under section 166 for the same death
If they pursue section 166, assess fault realistically: dense fog and a truck driver who could not see do not clear the driver
Make a fair settlement offer on the basis the family chooses, with earnings and dependency properly assessed
Do not exploit their uncertainty; record the advice given
assessment: Genuine fatal claim. The task is to handle the choice of remedy fairly and avoid double compensation, while recognising the driver probably bears fault.
action: Clarify the election of remedy and make a fair offer on the chosen route.
outcomes: Family withdraws the section 164 claim and settles under section 166 for ₹26 lakh
Family takes the ₹5 lakh quickly and closes the matter

title: The detailed accident report arrived on day 88, and the offer is due
type: Fatal accident where the insurer must make a settlement offer on the police report
story: Our policyholder's car hit a motorcyclist, Imran Sheikh, aged 38, at a junction in Indore; he died in hospital. The police filed the Detailed Accident Report with the claims tribunal 88 days after the accident and served a copy on the insurer. The report records his income as ₹45,000 a month from a mobile repair shop. No income tax returns are on file; his bank statements show average deposits of about ₹18,000 a month. The insurer's designated officer has not yet acted, and 24 of the 30 days for an offer have passed.
statement: (Widow) His shop was always full, he repaired phones for the whole market. He kept most of the money in cash, he didn't trust banks. We have three children. My husband was everything to us.

accounts.text: Accident at a junction; car driver failed to yield. Deceased aged 38, self-employed, monthly income stated by the family as ₹45,000. Dependants: widow, three minor children. Documents: bank statements; no income tax returns.
Savings account in the deceased's name, 24 months: average monthly credits ₹18,200, mostly cash deposits.

whatHappened: A genuine fatal accident caused by our policyholder. The stated income is higher than the evidence supports, and the insurer is close to missing its time limit for an offer.
damage: Death of a 38-year-old self-employed earner with four dependants.
missing: Shop rent agreement or trade licence
GST or other business records
inconsistencies: Income stated at ₹45,000 a month; bank credits average ₹18,200
indicators: Income stated without documentary support
innocent: Small traders often keep income in cash and do not file returns
questions: Ask for the shop’s rent agreement, trade licence and any supplier invoices
steps: Make the designated officer’s offer before the 30 days from receipt of the report run out
Base income on the evidence, with a reasoned view of cash income, rather than the stated ₹45,000

Calculate dependency in the standard way: income plus future prospects for a self-employed person under 40, a deduction for personal expenses for four dependants, the multiplier for age 38, and the conventional heads
Present the offer to the tribunal with the reasoning, so it can be accepted or adjudicated quickly
assessment: Genuine fatal claim with an overstated income. The urgent risk is procedural: missing the 30-day offer window.
action: Make a reasoned offer within the deadline on evidence-based income.
outcomes: Offer on ₹24,000 a month accepted before the tribunal
Tribunal fixes income at ₹27,000 and awards accordingly

title: Two lakh from the hit-and-run fund, then the car was found
type: Hit-and-run death compensated by the scheme before the vehicle was traced
story: Gopal Das, a 61-year-old pedestrian, was killed in Bhubaneswar by a car that did not stop. His family received ₹2 lakh under the hit-and-run compensation scheme. Seven months later the police traced the car from CCTV; it is insured with us. The family has filed a claim before the motor accident claims tribunal for full compensation against the owner and the insurer.
statement: (Son) We were told the driver would never be found, so we took the two lakh. Now the police have the car and the driver. My father ran a tea stall and supported my mother. We want full compensation now.

accounts.text: Compensation of ₹2,00,000 sanctioned for death in a hit-and-run accident, the vehicle being unidentified. Undertaking furnished by the claimants to refund the amount if compensation is later awarded for the same accident.
Offending car identified through CCTV seven months after the accident. Owner and driver traced; driver arrested. Vehicle insured on the date of the accident.

whatHappened: A genuine fatal hit-and-run, compensated by the scheme while the vehicle was unknown. Now that it is traced, the family can claim full compensation, but the scheme payment must be refunded or adjusted.
damage: Death of a 61-year-old tea stall owner.
thirdParties: The owner and driver of the traced car
evidence: Commissioner’s order with the refund undertaking
missing: Proof of the deceased’s income
innocent: Families rightly take scheme payments when the driver is unknown
questions: Confirm the policy was in force and the driver was licensed
steps: Handle the tribunal claim on merit: the vehicle was insured and the policy applies
Ask the tribunal to direct that the ₹2 lakh already paid by the scheme be refunded to it from the award, as the family undertook
Assess dependency fairly on the evidence of his income
Explain the adjustment to the family so it does not feel like a deduction taken by the insurer
assessment: Genuine and now payable under the policy. The scheme payment is not lost to the family but must be refunded from the award, avoiding double compensation.
action: Defend or settle on merit and provide for the refund of the scheme payment from the award.
outcomes: Award of ₹9.4 lakh with ₹2 lakh refunded to the scheme
Settled before the tribunal with the refund built in

title: A dented roof on a brand-new Seltos, and two companies blaming each other
type: New car damaged in delivery; recovery disputed between transporter and dealer
story: Policyholder bought a new Kia Seltos from a dealer in Kochi with home delivery. His policy started on the invoice date. A transport company delivered the car on a car carrier. At delivery he noticed a dented roof and a scratched door. The transporter says the damage happened in the dealer's yard; the dealer says the car left the yard perfect. He has claimed under his policy and the insurer wants to recover the cost from whoever is responsible.
statement: The roof was dented right above the driver's door, like something hit it from above. I wrote "damaged, subject to inspection" on the delivery note before I signed. I don't care who pays as long as my new car is fixed properly.

accounts.text: Four photos time-stamped at dispatch, showing the car from both sides. Roof not visible in any photo. Doors on the visible side unmarked.
Loaded at dealer's yard at 10:15. Delivered at 15:40. Customer remark: "Roof dented, door scratched, subject to inspection." Driver remark: "Damage present at loading."

whatHappened: The damage happened before or during delivery. Whether it was at the yard or on the carrier is genuinely unclear, but either way the policyholder did not cause it.
damage: Seltos: roof dent above the driver's door and a scratched rear door; estimate ₹68,000 including roof repaint.
missing: The car carrier’s upper deck layout and loading photos
Yard CCTV
inconsistencies: The driver says the damage was present at loading; the dealer says the car left perfect, but its photos do not show the roof
innocent: Roof damage from an upper-deck car carrier and yard knocks both happen
questions: Ask the transporter which deck the car travelled on and for loading photos
Ask the dealer for yard CCTV
steps: Pay the policyholder’s repair: the loss happened after the policy started and he did not cause it
Serve a written notice of claim on both the transporter and the dealer promptly, preserving recovery rights, including under carriage law against the transporter
Use the roof-shaped dent, deck position and CCTV to decide where the damage occurred
Pursue recovery against the party the evidence points to, or settle a split if it remains unclear
assessment: Disputed between two businesses, not with the customer. Pay him promptly and pursue recovery on the evidence.
action: Settle the claim and serve notice on both the transporter and the dealer.
outcomes: Transporter’s loading photos show an upper-deck strike; full recovery
Recovery shared 50/50 after neither side’s evidence settles it

title: Five accidents, five cars that were scrapped last year
type: Claims on cars whose registrations belong to scrapped vehicles
story: Policyholder claims ₹3.8 lakh for a 2017 Honda City damaged in a crash into a divider near Ghaziabad. The policy was bought online with an uploaded RC copy. A Vahan check shows the chassis number belongs to a car deregistered at a registered vehicle scrapping facility last year, with a certificate of deposit issued. The claims team has found four other claims in six months with the same pattern, all repaired at the same garage and all linked to the same mobile number.
statement: I bought this car second-hand from a man in Meerut, I have the papers. I don't know anything about any scrapping. The garage is near my house, everybody uses it. Please send the surveyor again if you don't believe me.

accounts.text: Chassis number status: scrapped. Certificate of deposit issued by a registered vehicle scrapping facility 11 months before the policy. Registration cancelled.

Five own-damage claims in six months: all policies bought online with uploaded RC copies; all chassis numbers match scrapped vehicles; all repaired at the same garage in Ghaziabad; the same mobile number appears as alternate contact on four policies. Surveyor photos show chassis number plates with fresh rivets.

whatHappened: An organised group is insuring cars carrying the identities of scrapped vehicles, using forged RCs, and claiming for staged damage through one garage.
damage: Claimed ₹3.8 lakh for front end damage. Four related claims total about ₹14 lakh.
thirdParties: The person behind the shared mobile number
evidence: Vahan records for all five vehicles
Surveyor's photos of the chassis plates
missing: The scrapping facility’s records of what happened to the scrapped bodies and plates
The real engine and chassis numbers stamped on the car
inconsistencies: The uploaded RC shows an active registration; Vahan shows the vehicle scrapped and the registration cancelled
indicators: Identity of a scrapped vehicle
Fresh rivets on the chassis number plate
Linked claims through one garage and one mobile number
innocent: A buyer could unknowingly purchase a re-plated car, but not five times through the same garage
questions: Have the actual chassis and engine numbers stamped on the car read by an expert
Ask the policyholder for the seller’s details and the payment record
steps: Hold all five claims and refer them together to the fraud investigation unit
Inspect the vehicles for the stamped numbers and compare them with Vahan
Report to the police and the transport authority, and alert the scrapping facility
Cancel the policies obtained on forged documents and share the pattern through industry fraud channels
assessment: Organised fraud: scrapped identities, forged registration documents and a common garage across five claims.
action: Hold and investigate all five claims together, report to the police, and void the policies.
outcomes: Police find a workshop re-plating salvage cars; claims repudiated
Garage owner and two agents arrested

title: Six lakh of bills from a nursing home with no registration
type: Injury claim before the tribunal supported by fabricated hospital bills
story: A motorcyclist injured when our policyholder's car clipped him in Meerut has claimed ₹6.2 lakh of medical expenses before the claims tribunal, with bills from "Shree Sai Nursing Home". The government hospital's medico-legal record shows he was treated there for a fractured wrist and discharged after two days. The nursing home does not appear in the state register of clinical establishments, and its bill numbers run in sequence with bills filed in two other unrelated claims.
statement: (Claimant's lawyer) After the government hospital my client was shifted to a private nursing home for proper treatment, surgery and physiotherapy for three weeks. The bills are genuine and proved by the treating doctor's certificate.

accounts.text: Admitted on the day of the accident with a fracture of the right radius. Closed reduction and plaster cast. Discharged after two days with advice to attend the fracture clinic. No referral to any private facility recorded.

"Shree Sai Nursing Home": not found in the state register of clinical establishments; address is a residential flat. Treating doctor's registration number belongs to a dentist registered in another state. Bill numbers 1187 to 1191 used here; bills 1185 and 1192 filed in two other tribunal claims on different dates.

whatHappened: A genuine accident and a real wrist fracture treated at a government hospital. The nursing home treatment and bills were fabricated to inflate the claim.
damage: Fractured right radius treated with a cast. Claimed medical expenses ₹6.2 lakh; real expenses minimal.
thirdParties: The purported nursing home and doctor
evidence: Verification report on the nursing home and doctor
missing: The fracture clinic follow-up records
X-rays from any private facility
inconsistencies: The lawyer says surgery was done at the nursing home; the government hospital treated the fracture with a cast and recorded no referral
indicators: Unregistered facility at a residential address
Doctor's registration belongs to a dentist in another state
Bill numbers shared with other claims
innocent: A claimant can be misled by a tout who arranges paperwork, but the bills still cannot be paid
questions: Put the verification report to the claimant through the tribunal
Ask for the X-rays and implant details of the claimed surgery
steps: Contest the medical expenses before the tribunal with the verification report and the government hospital record
Accept the genuine injury: pay compensation for the wrist fracture on the real medical evidence
Link the two other claims with the same bill series and review them
Report the fabricated bills to the police and the medical council
assessment: Third-party fraud on the medical expenses; the underlying injury is real. Pay what is genuine and contest the fabricated bills.
action: Contest the bills with the verification evidence, pay the genuine injury claim, and report the fabrication.
outcomes: Tribunal rejects the bills and awards ₹85,000 for the fracture
Police raid finds a bill-making racket supplying several lawyers

title: Sold on stamp paper, then reported stolen
type: Theft claim for a vehicle sold privately but not transferred
story: Policyholder reported his Toyota Innova stolen from outside a temple in Guntur and an FIR was registered. FASTag records show the vehicle crossing toll plazas between Guntur and Chennai nine times in the five weeks after the reported theft. Two e-challans for speeding were issued to it in Chennai. A used-car dealer has told the investigator that the policyholder sold the car to a buyer on a stamp-paper agreement four months earlier, with the loan to be cleared later.
statement: I parked at the temple and when I came out it was gone. I don't know who is driving it. I never sold it, the RC is in my name. Some dealers spread stories. Please settle quickly, the bank is calling me about the loan.

accounts.text: Nine toll crossings between Guntur and Chennai in the five weeks after the reported theft, all on the vehicle's FASTag, which is still recharged from a UPI account. Two speeding e-challans issued in Chennai after the theft date.

He sold the Innova through me four months ago to a man from Chennai, on a hundred-rupee stamp paper agreement. The buyer was to pay the balance and clear the loan, then transfer the RC. I heard the buyer stopped paying.

whatHappened: He sold the car informally, the buyer stopped paying, and he reported it stolen to recover the money from the insurer.
damage: Claimed theft of an Innova; IDV ₹14,20,000. Vehicle in use in Chennai.
missing: The stamp paper agreement
The UPI account holder who recharges the FASTag
inconsistencies: He says he never sold the car; the dealer says he sold it four months before the theft
The car has been crossing tolls and collecting challans since it was "stolen"
indicators: Vehicle in regular use after the reported theft
FASTag still recharged
Private sale without transfer
Loan pressure
innocent: A buyer who stops paying can leave a seller desperate, but that is not a theft covered by the policy
questions: Ask him directly about the sale and the agreement
Identify the UPI account recharging the FASTag
steps: Put the dealer’s account and the toll records to him and take a written statement
Trace the vehicle through the FASTag and challan data and inform the police
Repudiate the theft claim if the sale is confirmed: there was no theft, and he had parted with the car
Report a false theft claim through the proper channels
assessment: Potential fraud with strong evidence: the car is being driven openly, and a witness describes a private sale.
action: Investigate the sale, help the police trace the car, and repudiate if confirmed.
outcomes: Car traced to the buyer; claim withdrawn
Claim repudiated and FIR closed as false

title: Surveyor on day 3, report on day 28, no decision on day 48
type: Own-damage claim handled outside the regulator’s timelines
story: Policyholder intimated an own-damage claim on 1 July after her car was rear-ended in heavy rain in Pune. A surveyor was appointed on 4 July and inspected the car on 6 July. The survey report was submitted on 29 July. On 18 August there is still no decision. She raised a grievance with the insurer on 1 August and has had no reply, and has now registered a complaint on the Bima Bharosa portal.
statement: My car has been sitting at the garage for seven weeks. Every time I call, I'm told the file is under process. I have sent every document they asked for. I'm paying for cabs every day. Isn't there a rule about how long this can take?

accounts.text: 1 July: claim intimated. 4 July: surveyor appointed. 6 July: survey. 29 July: final survey report received. 1 August: grievance received, no response logged. 18 August: no decision. All documents received by 8 July.
Complaint registered against the insurer for delay in claim settlement. Insurer to resolve and update the portal.

whatHappened: A straightforward genuine claim delayed at every stage, in breach of the regulator's timelines.
damage: Her Baleno: rear bumper, boot lid and tail lamps; surveyor's assessment ₹72,000.
missing: Any reason recorded for the delays
innocent: Monsoon claim volumes can overwhelm surveyors, but that does not suspend the timelines
questions: Check whether other monsoon claims are similarly delayed
steps: Decide and settle the claim now on the survey report
Record the breaches: the surveyor should be appointed within 24 hours, the report submitted within 15 days of the survey, and the claim decided within 7 days of the report
Pay interest for the delay as the regulations require, and respond to the grievance and the Bima Bharosa complaint with what was done
Find out why the grievance went unanswered and fix the queue
assessment: Genuine claim and clear regulatory breaches by the insurer. Settle, compensate the delay and answer the complaint.
action: Settle now with interest, respond on Bima Bharosa, and fix the delays.
outcomes: Settled with interest within 3 days; complaint closed
Review finds 300 monsoon claims past the 7-day decision limit

title: ₹72,000 cut from a zero-depreciation claim with no explanation
type: Partial settlement with unexplained deductions, heading for the ombudsman
story: Policyholder's SUV was hit on its side at a junction in Kochi. His policy has a zero-depreciation add-on. The repair bill was ₹2,10,000 and the insurer paid ₹1,38,000. The settlement letter lists three deductions without detail: "depreciation ₹42,000", "not related to accident ₹18,000" and "labour cut ₹12,000". He wrote to the grievance cell 40 days ago and has had no reply. He is preparing a complaint to the Insurance Ombudsman.
statement: I paid extra every year for zero dep precisely so this wouldn't happen. Nobody has told me what "not related to accident" means. The surveyor saw the car with me. I've written to them, nobody answers. I'll go to the ombudsman if I have to.

accounts.text: Repair invoice ₹2,10,000. Less: depreciation ₹42,000; not related to accident ₹18,000; labour cut ₹12,000. Amount paid ₹1,38,000. Policy add-ons: zero depreciation.
Grievance received 40 days ago asking for a breakdown of the deductions. Status: open, unassigned.

whatHappened: A genuine claim underpaid. The depreciation deduction ignores his zero-depreciation add-on, and the other deductions were never explained.
damage: Mahindra XUV700: front door, rear door, B-pillar trim and side mirror; repair ₹2,10,000.
missing: The surveyor's working for the ₹18,000 and the labour cut
inconsistencies: Depreciation deducted on a policy with a zero-depreciation add-on
innocent: A settlement system may apply depreciation by default if the add-on is not read from the policy
questions: Ask the surveyor which parts were treated as not related to the accident and why
steps: Refund the ₹42,000 depreciation: the zero-depreciation add-on covers it
Review the other deductions against the survey report and give a written, item-by-item explanation; refund any not supported
Answer his grievance in writing now
Explain his right to approach the Insurance Ombudsman within a year of the insurer’s reply (or one month without a reply) for claims up to ₹50 lakh, and expect the deductions to be scrutinised there
assessment: Genuine and underpaid, with unexplained deductions and an ignored grievance. A clear ombudsman risk the insurer should fix itself.
action: Refund the depreciation, justify or refund the other deductions, and answer the grievance in writing.
outcomes: ₹54,000 refunded with an item-wise explanation; ombudsman complaint not filed
Ombudsman awards the full difference

title: A thumbprint on "full and final" at the garage counter
type: Discharge voucher signed by a vulnerable customer under pressure
story: Policyholder, aged 64, from a village near Gaya, Bihar, owns a car driven by her son for the family business. After it hit a tree, the surveyor assessed the loss at ₹1,10,000 and the garage bill came to ₹1,08,000. At the garage, the surveyor gave her a discharge voucher for ₹62,000 marked "full and final" and told her she would not get the car back unless she signed. She cannot read English and put her thumbprint on it. She now wants the balance.
statement: (Through her son) The sahib said sign here or the car stays here. I don't read English. I thought it was the paper to take the car home. When the money came it was only sixty-two thousand. The garage took the rest from my son.

accounts.text: Assessed loss ₹1,10,000 net of depreciation and excess. Recommended for settlement.
"I accept ₹62,000 in full and final settlement of all claims under the policy." Thumb impression of the insured. Witness: the surveyor. Printed in English only.

whatHappened: A genuine claim underpaid by ₹48,000 through a voucher obtained from an elderly customer who could not read it, under pressure.
damage: Maruti Ertiga: front bumper, radiator, bonnet and headlamps. Garage bill ₹1,08,000; surveyor assessment ₹1,10,000.
missing: Why the voucher amount differs from the surveyor’s own assessment
inconsistencies: The surveyor assessed ₹1,10,000 but witnessed a voucher for ₹62,000
innocent: A clerical error could explain the figure, but not the pressure to sign or the English-only form for a customer who cannot read it
questions: Ask the surveyor to explain the ₹62,000 figure and the circumstances of the signing
steps: Do not rely on the voucher: a discharge signed under pressure by a customer who could not read it does not prevent her claiming the balance, and forums treat such vouchers sceptically
Pay the balance of the assessed loss with interest for the delay
Investigate the surveyor’s conduct and report it if confirmed
Communicate with her in Hindi, through her son if she wishes, and check whether other customers were treated the same way
assessment: Genuine claim and a vulnerable customer who was pressured into an unfair discharge. The insurer should correct it before a consumer forum does.
action: Pay the ₹48,000 balance with interest and investigate the surveyor.
outcomes: Balance paid; surveyor removed from the panel
Review finds three more vouchers obtained the same way

title: Details swapped on a Brampton street, and no report to the collision centre
type: Collision not reported to police or a collision reporting centre
story: Policyholder and another driver collided at a residential intersection in Brampton, Ontario, on an icy evening. They exchanged names and phone numbers and drove away. Neither reported the collision to the police or a collision reporting centre, although the combined damage is clearly over $2,000. Three weeks later he made a claim. The other driver now says the policyholder slid into her and that she will claim against him.
statement: We were both shaken and it was getting dark, so we took photos of each other's licences and left. I didn't know we had to go to the reporting centre. She was the one who slid through the stop sign, I was already in the intersection. Now she's changing her story.

accounts.text: Six photos time-stamped at the scene: both cars at the intersection, the other car's front bumper against the policyholder's rear passenger door, the other driver's licence, and the stop sign on her side of the intersection.
He came through the intersection too fast for the ice and slid into the front of my car. I had stopped at my sign. I will be making a claim.

whatHappened: A genuine collision that should have been reported within 24 hours. The photos are the strongest evidence of where each car was.
damage: His Civic: rear passenger door and quarter panel, $4,100. Her car: front bumper and headlamp, about $2,300.
thirdParties: The other driver and her insurer
evidence: Other driver's statement through her insurer
missing: A collision report
Any doorbell or dashcam footage from nearby houses
inconsistencies: Each driver says the other slid into them
innocent: Many drivers do not know that a collision with over $2,000 of damage must be reported
questions: Ask both drivers to report the collision now at a collision reporting centre
Ask neighbours on the intersection for doorbell footage
steps: Ask him to report the collision now; late reporting is a legal issue, not a bar to his claim
Use the photo of the impact point: her bumper against his rear door is consistent with her car striking his side, which supports his account
Apply Ontario’s Fault Determination Rules to the positions and the stop sign, and handle his damage under the coverages on his policy
Respond to her claim through her insurer using the same evidence
assessment: Genuine collision, not reported as required. The photos support his account; the reporting failure weakens the evidence but does not defeat the claim.
action: Have the collision reported now, decide fault on the photos and the rules, and handle both claims.
outcomes: Fault assigned to the other driver under the rules; claim paid
Doorbell footage confirms she rolled through the stop sign

title: A two-year-old leased SUV, valued as if it were used
type: Total loss settlement ignoring an endorsement that removes depreciation
story: Policyholder's leased SUV was written off in a three-car collision on Highway 7 in Vaughan, 20 months after she leased it new. Her policy includes the Ontario endorsement that removes the depreciation deduction for a vehicle leased new, for a set period after delivery. The adjuster offered the actual cash value of $41,000. The vehicle's original price was $52,400, and the leasing company is the loss payee.
statement: I paid extra for the no-depreciation endorsement because I knew a new car loses value fast. The broker said if it was written off in the first two years I'd get the full price. Now I'm offered $41,000 and the leasing company says I still owe them more than that.

accounts.text: Endorsement: removing depreciation deduction, leased vehicle. Vehicle leased new 20 months before the loss. Lessor shown as loss payee.
Actual cash value from comparable listings: $41,000, less deductible. Endorsement not referred to.

whatHappened: A genuine total loss within the endorsement period. The offer applied ordinary actual cash value and ignored the endorsement she paid for.
damage: SUV total loss.
thirdParties: The leasing company (lessor and loss payee)
missing: The lessor's payout statement
inconsistencies: The policy carries the endorsement; the offer ignores it
innocent: The total loss system may not pick up endorsements automatically
questions: Ask the leasing company for its payout figure
steps: Settle under the endorsement terms instead of actual cash value, since the loss is within the endorsement period
Pay the lessor as loss payee first, then any balance to her
Explain the calculation in writing and apologize for the first offer
Check other recent total losses for the same omission
assessment: Genuine and covered on better terms than offered. The endorsement she paid for applies.
action: Re-settle under the removing depreciation endorsement and pay the lessor and her accordingly.
outcomes: Re-settled at the original price; lessor paid and balance to her
Review finds four other files with the same error

title: Hit by a red-light runner in Kelowna, and told she cannot sue him
type: Injury claim under British Columbia’s no-fault Enhanced Care model
story: Policyholder was injured in Kelowna, British Columbia, when another driver ran a red light and hit her car. She has a fractured collarbone and cannot work as a dental hygienist for at least ten weeks. A friend in Alberta told her to hire a lawyer and sue the other driver for pain and suffering. She has asked her insurer why the claim is being handled through accident benefits only.
statement: He ran the red light, there's a witness and the police ticketed him. Why should I just get benefits? My friend in Calgary got a big settlement for less than this. I want him to pay for what he did to me.

accounts.text: Vehicle 2 entered the intersection against a red light and struck vehicle 1. Driver of vehicle 2 issued a violation ticket. Independent witness statement attached.

Accident occurred after May 2021: Enhanced Care benefits apply. Medical and rehabilitation benefits, income replacement at 90% of net income up to the statutory maximum, and a permanent impairment benefit if applicable.

whatHappened: A genuine not-at-fault injury in British Columbia, where the Enhanced Care model replaced most lawsuits for injuries with care-based benefits.
damage: Fractured collarbone, ten weeks off work. Car: front-left damage.
missing: Her pay records for the income replacement calculation
innocent: Rules differ sharply between provinces, and advice from Alberta does not apply in BC
questions: Ask for her pay records and her physiotherapy plan
steps: Explain that in BC, for accidents since May 2021, the right to sue an at-fault driver for injuries has been removed in most cases and replaced by care-based benefits
Pay her benefits promptly: treatment, income replacement and any impairment benefit
Tell her how to request a review if she disagrees with a benefit decision
Record the other driver as at fault for her vehicle damage and premium purposes
assessment: Genuine and covered under Enhanced Care benefits. Her wish to sue is understandable but generally not available in BC.
action: Explain the model clearly, pay all benefits she is entitled to, and set out the review route.
outcomes: Benefits paid; she returns to work after 11 weeks
Review request on income replacement partly upheld

title: Changing lanes on the Queensway, rated 100% at fault
type: Customer dispute about a fault determination, escalated through the complaint process
story: Policyholder was changing lanes on the Queensway in Ottawa when a car in the next lane hit his rear quarter. Under Ontario's Fault Determination Rules for a lane change, he has been rated 100% at fault, which will affect his premium. He says the other driver sped up to close the gap. He complained to the insurer, was unhappy with the reply, and asked how to take it further.
statement: I signalled for five seconds, there was a big gap. He saw me and floored it to stop me getting in. The dashcam shows him speeding up. How can a rule say I'm 100% at fault when he did it on purpose?

accounts.text: Indicator on for about five seconds before the lane change. The following car's headlights grow quickly in the frame in the last two seconds, consistent with it accelerating. Contact at the rear quarter as the lane change completes.

Fault has been determined under Ontario Regulation 668, the Fault Determination Rules. A vehicle changing lanes that collides with a vehicle in the other lane is 100% at fault. We cannot change this determination.

whatHappened: A lane-change collision where the other driver probably accelerated to block him. The Fault Determination Rules still put the lane-changing driver at fault for rating and direct compensation purposes.
damage: His Camry: rear quarter and bumper, $3,300. Other car: front corner.
thirdParties: The other driver and their insurer
missing: Any witness who saw the other car accelerate
inconsistencies: He says the other driver accelerated deliberately; the rules take no account of that
innocent: Customers reasonably expect fault to reflect what actually happened
questions: Ask whether he wants to report the other driver’s conduct to the police
steps: Explain clearly and without jargon that the Fault Determination Rules apply as written for rating and his own damage, whatever the other driver’s conduct
Note that the rules do not decide fault in a lawsuit, and that dangerous driving can be reported to the police
Escalate his complaint to the insurer’s internal ombudsman if he remains unhappy, and then explain his right to go to the General Insurance OmbudService and the regulator
Keep the dashcam on file in case it becomes relevant to any injury claim
assessment: Genuinely disputed in fairness, but the rule is applied correctly. Good handling means a clear explanation and an open path for his complaint.
action: Maintain the rule-based determination, explain it plainly, and guide him through the escalation route.
outcomes: Complaint closed after the internal ombudsman explains the rules
General Insurance OmbudService finds the rules were applied correctly

title: Bought on Marketplace, insured for four months, stolen all along
type: Collision claim reveals the insured vehicle is a re-VINned stolen car
story: Policyholder bought a two-year-old Toyota Highlander through an online marketplace in Laval, Quebec, for $38,000 in cash, and insured it. Four months later he rear-ended a car on an icy road and claimed for both. The appraiser noticed the public VIN plate had been re-riveted. A check of the hidden secondary VIN shows the vehicle was stolen in Mississauga, Ontario, five months before he bought it. The VIN on his paperwork belongs to a Highlander that was written off in Alberta.
statement: The seller met me at a mall, showed me the registration and a clean history report for the VIN. I paid cash because he said the bank transfer would take days. I had no idea. I've lost $38,000 and now you're telling me the car isn't even mine.

accounts.text: Public VIN plate shows non-factory rivets. Secondary VIN read from a concealed location does not match. Secondary VIN reported stolen in Ontario five months before the purchase. Public VIN belongs to a vehicle recorded as a total loss in Alberta.
Handwritten bill of sale, $38,000 cash. Copy of a registration in the seller's name bearing the cloned VIN. Vehicle history report for the cloned VIN, showing no accidents.

whatHappened: He is the victim of a re-VINning scheme: he bought a stolen vehicle disguised with the identity of a written-off car.
damage: Highlander: front end, $7,800. Other car: rear bumper and trunk, $4,200.
thirdParties: The original owner and their insurer
missing: The seller’s real identity
The original owner’s insurer and whether it paid a theft claim
inconsistencies: The paperwork VIN belongs to a written-off vehicle; the hidden VIN belongs to a stolen one
indicators: Re-riveted VIN plate
Cash sale in a mall car park
History report run on the cloned VIN
innocent: Clean history reports on a cloned VIN fool many buyers
questions: Ask for any messages with the seller and the listing
Identify the original owner’s insurer
steps: Treat the policyholder as a fraud victim and help him report to the police
Notify the police and the original owner’s insurer; the vehicle belongs to the original owner or to the insurer that paid its theft claim
Get advice on the third party’s claim: he was insured as the driver of that vehicle, and the person he hit should not be left without a remedy
Decline the own-damage claim, since he has no ownership interest in the stolen vehicle, and refund the premium for the vehicle cover
assessment: The policyholder is genuine and a victim; the vehicle is stolen. Ownership, not his honesty, decides the own-damage claim.
action: Report the stolen vehicle, deal fairly with the third party, decline own damage and refund the premium.
outcomes: Vehicle returned to the original owner’s insurer; third party paid; premium refunded
Police link the seller to a ring that re-VINned 40 vehicles

title: The other driver gave a name, a number, and a car he no longer owned
type: Claim under an uninsured motorist extension with an unverified at-fault driver
story: Policyholder has a third party property policy with an uninsured motorist extension, which pays up to $5,000 for her car's damage if an identified, uninsured driver is at fault. Her car was rear-ended at lights in Brisbane in heavy rain. The other driver gave a name and mobile number, which no longer answers. The plate she photographed is registered to a woman who says she sold the car two months ago and the buyer never transferred the registration.
statement: He was really apologetic, he said he had no insurance and would pay me himself. I took a photo of his plate and his car. Now his number's dead. The repair quote is $6,800. I only have third party cover because I can't afford comprehensive.

accounts.text: I sold that car on an online marketplace two months ago for cash. I filled in my half of the transfer form and gave the buyer the rest. He obviously never lodged it. I have a screenshot of our messages and his first name.

Uninsured motorist extension: we pay up to $5,000 for damage to your car if the other driver was at fault, did not have insurance, and you can give us their name and address or the vehicle's registration details.

whatHappened: A genuine rear-end collision by an uninsured driver. The extension may apply, but the at-fault driver's identity is not yet established.
damage: Her Mazda 3: rear bumper, boot and tail lamps, quote $6,800.
thirdParties: The registered operator who sold the car
evidence: Photo of the other car and its plate
Registered operator's statement and sale messages
missing: The buyer’s full name and address
A police report
innocent: Unlodged registration transfers after private sales are common
questions: Ask the registered operator for the buyer’s messages and payment details
Ask the policyholder to report the collision to the police
steps: Check the wording: the extension can be met with the vehicle’s registration details and evidence the driver was at fault and uninsured
Help identify the buyer through the sale messages and a police report
If the conditions are met, pay up to the $5,000 limit; explain that the rest can only be pursued against the driver
Keep her informed while the identification is attempted
assessment: Insufficient evidence for now, with a genuine policyholder. The registration and photo may be enough under the wording; identifying the buyer would settle it.
action: Pursue the buyer's identity, assess the extension on the registration evidence, and pay up to the limit if met.
outcomes: Buyer identified through the sale messages; $5,000 paid and recovery pursued
Paid on the registration evidence alone under the wording

title: Lodged in February, still undecided in June
type: Claim handled outside the General Insurance Code of Practice timeframes
story: Policyholder lodged a comprehensive claim on 3 February after his parked car was hit in a shopping centre car park in Adelaide. An assessor was appointed but he was not told for three weeks. He received no updates for nine weeks. He complained on 1 June and has had no response. On 20 June, more than four months after lodgement, there is no decision and no exceptional circumstances are recorded.
statement: It's a straightforward scrape, the centre's CCTV shows the other car. I've rung every fortnight and I'm told it's with the assessor. I complained in writing three weeks ago and heard nothing. I've been driving around with a door held shut with tape.

accounts.text: 3 Feb: claim lodged. 10 Feb: assessor appointed; customer told 3 Mar. Assessor report received 28 Mar. No customer update between 3 Mar and 5 May. 1 Jun: written complaint received, not acknowledged. 20 Jun: no decision. Exceptional circumstances: none recorded.
Footage supplied 14 Feb showing a white ute reversing into the policyholder's car and leaving. Plate partly legible.

whatHappened: A straightforward claim left without a decision, updates or a complaint response, in breach of the Code's timeframes.
damage: His Corolla: driver's door and rear door dented; door does not close; quote $3,400.
missing: The reason no decision was made after the assessor’s report
innocent: Assessor backlogs after storms delay many claims, but the Code still applies
questions: Check whether the ute driver can be identified from the partial plate for recovery
steps: Decide the claim now: all the information has been on file since late March
Record the Code breaches: late notice of the assessor, no updates at least every 20 business days, no decision within 10 business days of having the information or within 4 months
Respond to the complaint in writing within the Code’s complaint timeframe, and tell him he can take it to AFCA if unhappy
Consider compensation for the delay and fix the update process
assessment: Genuine and overdue. The insurer has breached several Code timeframes and should decide, apologize and explain the AFCA route.
action: Approve the claim now, respond to the complaint with the AFCA option, and address the delay.
outcomes: Claim approved the same week; complaint closed with a goodwill payment
AFCA complaint finds the delays unreasonable

title: Her ex-partner smashed the car, and he is still on the policy
type: Deliberate damage by a co-insured ex-partner in a family violence situation
story: Policyholder holds a comprehensive policy on which her former partner is still listed as a named driver and joint policyholder. After they separated, he smashed the windscreen and lights and scratched the panels of the car outside her home in Geelong. Police attended and a family violence intervention order is now in place. She has claimed for the damage. The claims team has flagged the policy's exclusion for damage caused intentionally by "you or anyone acting with your consent".
statement: I just need the car fixed so I can get the kids to school. I didn't know he was still on the policy, we set it up together years ago. Please don't contact him about this. He doesn't know where I'm staying some nights.
