accounts.text: Attended a family violence incident. Respondent damaged the protected person's vehicle with a steering lock: windscreen, headlights and both doors damaged. Intervention order applied for and granted. Respondent charged with criminal damage.

Joint policyholders: Sarah Mitchell and Jason Mitchell. Premiums paid from her account for the last two years. Exclusion: loss or damage caused intentionally by you or a person acting with your express or implied consent.

whatHappened: The damage was deliberate family violence by her former partner. She did not cause or consent to it.
damage: Kia Cerato: windscreen, headlights, scratched doors and panels; quote $5,900.
thirdParties: Jason Mitchell, the former partner and respondent
missing: Her preferred safe contact method
innocent: Joint policies set up during a relationship are often never updated after separation
questions: Ask her how and when it is safe to contact her
steps: Apply the insurer’s family violence policy under the Code: do not apply the intentional damage exclusion against a victim who did not cause or consent to the damage
Pay her claim without contacting the former partner or disclosing her details or location to him
Remove him from the policy at her request and update her contact details securely
Offer support referrals, flexible payment of any excess, and a single contact who knows her situation
assessment: Genuine, and a customer experiencing family violence. The exclusion should not be used against the victim; safety and discretion come first.
action: Pay the claim, keep her details from the perpetrator, and remove him from the policy.
outcomes: Claim paid in a week; former partner removed from the policy
Insurer pursues recovery from him through the courts without involving her

title: A cash offer at the insurer’s rates, and a quote that includes old hail
type: Cash settlement dispute where the customer’s quote includes unrelated damage
story: Policyholder reversed into a concrete pole in a Perth car park, damaging his rear bumper and tailgate. He asked for a cash settlement. The insurer offered $4,200, based on its preferred repairer's rates. His own repairer quoted $7,900. That quote includes paintless dent repair across the roof and bonnet, and the assessor's photos show hail dents that match a storm two years ago, which he never claimed.
statement: My repairer is who I trust, and he says $4,200 won't cover it. Your repairers get discounts I can't get. I don't see why I should be out of pocket. The hail dents were always there, I just thought they'd do them while it was in.

accounts.text: Collision damage: rear bumper, tailgate, reversing sensor. Customer's quote includes $2,600 of roof and bonnet dent repair for hail damage not related to this incident. Insurer's offer uses preferred repairer labour rates about 20% below the customer's repairer.
Hailstorm over the policyholder's suburb two years before this claim. No hail claim lodged on this policy.

whatHappened: A genuine collision. The customer's quote adds unrelated hail damage, while the insurer's offer uses discounted rates he cannot get.
damage: Rear bumper, tailgate and reversing sensor. Separate old hail dents on the roof and bonnet.
missing: A breakdown of the insurer’s offer that the customer can check
inconsistencies: His quote presents hail repairs as part of this claim
indicators: Unrelated damage added to the repair quote
innocent: Customers often ask repairers to fix everything at once without thinking about what the claim covers
questions: Ask his repairer to requote for the collision damage only
steps: Remove the hail repairs from the quote: they are unrelated and were never claimed
Make a fair cash settlement for the collision damage that reflects what it would reasonably cost him, not only the insurer’s discounted rates, and explain how it was worked out
Give him the itemised breakdown and the option of a repair through the insurer instead of cash
Tell him he can lodge a separate hail claim if within the policy terms, or arrange that repair himself
assessment: Mixed. The hail damage should come out, but a cash offer at internal discount rates is not fair either.
action: Exclude the hail items, recalculate a fair cash figure, and explain it with an itemised breakdown.
outcomes: Cash settled at $5,050 after a collision-only requote
Customer chooses an insurer-arranged repair instead

title: "Free hail repair, no excess", from a pop-up in the car park
type: Hail claims lodged by a repair business that inflates and adds old damage
story: After a hailstorm in Melbourne's north, a repair business set up in a shopping centre car park offering "free hail repair, no excess". It lodged a claim on the policyholder's behalf under a signed authority, with an estimate of $11,400. The assessor found light hail dents on the roof, but the estimate also includes old door dings and a cracked bumper. Forty claims from the same business show near-identical estimates, and six of the cars are registered to addresses outside the hail zone.
statement: They said my insurance would cover it all and I wouldn't pay a cent. I signed their form on an iPad. I didn't know they'd put in the bumper, that crack's been there since my son reversed into the letterbox.

accounts.text: Light hail damage to the roof and bonnet consistent with the storm, fairly priced at about $3,200. Estimate also claims door dings with old paint wear and a cracked bumper with dirt in the crack. Dent repair rates in the estimate about double the local market.

Forty claims from the same business in two weeks. Estimate wording and line items near-identical. Six vehicles registered to suburbs outside the storm footprint. Excess "waived" by the business on every claim.

whatHappened: The policyholder has genuine light hail damage. The repair business inflated the estimate with old damage and inflated rates, and is doing so across many claims.
damage: Light hail dents to the roof and bonnet. Old door dings and a cracked bumper not caused by hail.
missing: Where the six out-of-area cars actually were during the storm
inconsistencies: The estimate attributes old door dings and a cracked bumper to hail
indicators: Excess waived as a sales offer
Near-identical estimates across forty claims
Cars outside the storm footprint
Rates double the market
innocent: Customers sign authorities quickly when promised a free repair
questions: Ask the policyholder whether she understood what the form allowed the business to do
Ask the six out-of-area owners where their cars were parked
steps: Pay the genuine hail damage at a fair rate, directly or through a repairer she chooses, and tell her what was excluded and why
Explain her excess remains payable under her policy; a waiver offered by the business does not change it
Refer the business’s claims as a group to the fraud team and review all forty
Report the conduct to the regulator if the investigation supports it
assessment: Potential fraud by the repairer, not the customer. Pay her genuine hail damage and investigate the business across all its claims.
action: Pay the fair hail cost, decline the old damage, and investigate the business's forty claims together.
outcomes: Business’s claims reduced across the portfolio; two referred to police
Customer chooses her own repairer for the hail work

title: A Patrol on the dunes near Al Faqa, and no off-road extension
type: Rollover while dune driving on a policy that excludes off-road use
story: Policyholder rolled his Nissan Patrol onto its roof while driving over dunes near Al Faqa on a weekend trip with friends. Nobody was hurt. A friend's 4x4 pulled the car back onto its wheels and a recovery truck took it to Dubai. His comprehensive policy excludes use off paved roads unless the optional off-road extension is bought, and it was not bought.
statement: Everyone goes to the dunes at the weekend, the car is built for it. I went over a crest a bit fast and the sand gave way. I thought comprehensive meant everything. The salesman never mentioned off-road. The roof is crushed and the pillars are bent.

accounts.text: Single vehicle overturned in a desert area off the paved road near Al Faqa. No injuries. No third party involved. Driver licensed.

Exclusion: loss or damage while the vehicle is being driven off paved roads, including desert and dune driving, unless the off-road extension is shown in the schedule. Schedule: off-road extension not purchased.

whatHappened: A genuine rollover during dune driving, which the policy clearly excludes without the extension he did not buy.
damage: Patrol: roof crushed, A and B pillars bent, windscreen and side glass broken; likely a total loss.
missing: Sales records showing whether the off-road extension was offered
innocent: Many buyers assume comprehensive cover includes dune driving
questions: Ask for the sales call recording or quote to see whether the extension was offered
steps: Decline the own-damage claim under the off-road exclusion, explaining the wording and the extension in plain language
Check the sales records: if the extension was never offered or explained, handle it as a complaint about the sale
Offer to add the extension at renewal
assessment: Genuine accident, not covered. The exclusion is clear and the extension was not bought.
action: Decline with a clear explanation and review how the policy was sold.
outcomes: Declined; he accepts after the wording is explained
Complaint about the sale upheld; goodwill contribution offered

title: Found scraped in the Marina car park, reported four days later
type: Damage by an unknown party, reported to police days after it was found
story: Policyholder says he found a long scrape and dent on his car's rear quarter when he returned to it in a residential car park in Dubai Marina. He obtained a police report for damage by an unknown party four days later, because he was travelling for work. The garage needs the police report to repair the car. The building's CCTV is kept for only three days and has been overwritten.
statement: I came back late, saw the scrape in the morning and had to fly to Riyadh the same day. I did the police report as soon as I landed back. It's a residents' car park, someone must have scraped it parking. There's yellow paint in the scratch.

accounts.text: Report of damage to a parked vehicle by an unknown party, registered four days after the stated date of discovery. Location: residential building car park, Dubai Marina. No witnesses identified.
CCTV retention is 72 hours. Footage for the date given has been overwritten. Car park access logs show the policyholder's tag entering the night before and leaving the following morning.

whatHappened: Probably genuine car park damage by an unknown driver, but the four-day gap means the CCTV is gone and the timing cannot be confirmed.
damage: Lexus IS: rear quarter scrape and dent with yellow paint transfer; estimate AED 4,800.
missing: CCTV of the incident
Whether any resident in the building drives a yellow car
indicators: Damage reported to police four days after discovery
innocent: Work travel explains the delay, and the access log supports his movements
questions: Ask building management whether any yellow vehicle is registered to the car park
Ask for his flight booking to confirm the travel
steps: Accept the police report as meeting the requirement for repair, and note the reason for the delay
Check the damage height and the yellow paint against the car park, for example yellow-painted pillars or barriers
If consistent, pay the claim as unknown-party damage under the comprehensive cover, applying any excess the policy sets for unknown third parties
Explain that reporting promptly preserves CCTV in future
assessment: Insufficient evidence rather than suspicion. The travel and the access log support his account; the damage pattern can be checked against the car park.
action: Inspect the paint transfer against the car park and pay as unknown-party damage if consistent.
outcomes: Yellow paint matches a column guard near his bay; claim paid
Paid after his flight booking confirms the trip

title: Agency repair until three years old, and the car is three years and two months
type: Dispute over agency repair entitlement based on vehicle age
story: Policyholder's Lexus ES was rear-ended at a signal in Abu Dhabi; the other driver was found at fault but she has claimed under her own comprehensive policy for speed. The claims team approved repair at a non-agency garage because the car is now three years and two months old and agency repair is "for vehicles up to three years". Her renewal schedule, issued two months before the accident, lists "Agency repair: Yes" for the policy year without any age condition.
statement: I renewed two months ago and the schedule says agency repair. Nobody told me it would stop halfway through the year. The car has always been serviced at the agency. I want it repaired there with genuine parts, that's what I paid for.

accounts.text: Period of insurance: 12 months from renewal. Repair condition: Agency repair: Yes. No age limit stated in the schedule.
Vehicle first registered 3 years 2 months before the accident. Underwriting guideline: agency repair up to 3 years. Approved non-agency repair.

whatHappened: A genuine claim where the internal guideline conflicts with the schedule the customer was given, which grants agency repair for the whole year.
damage: Lexus ES: rear bumper, boot lid and parking sensors; agency estimate AED 9,600, non-agency estimate AED 6,900.
thirdParties: The at-fault driver and their insurer
evidence: Police report finding the other driver at fault
missing: Any wording elsewhere in the policy that limits agency repair by age
inconsistencies: The schedule grants agency repair without an age limit; the internal guideline sets one
innocent: Underwriting guidelines are not always reflected in the documents issued to customers
questions: Check the full policy wording for any age condition on agency repair
steps: Honour agency repair for this policy period: the schedule issued to her grants it without an age condition, and an internal guideline cannot override her contract
Recover the cost from the at-fault driver’s insurer under the police report
Fix the renewal documents so that any age limit is stated clearly at renewal
assessment: Genuine claim and a fair complaint. The schedule she was given decides the entitlement.
action: Authorise the agency repair and recover from the at-fault driver's insurer.
outcomes: Agency repair authorised; full recovery from the other insurer
Renewal schedules updated to show age limits

title: A tourist in a rental car, a police report, and an insurer that will not pay
type: Recovery from a rental car’s insurer after a tourist contests fault
story: Policyholder's car was hit at a roundabout in Abu Dhabi by a rental car driven by a visiting tourist. The police report found the tourist at fault for entering without giving way. The insurer paid her repairs of AED 14,500 under her comprehensive cover and claimed the amount from the rental car's insurer. That insurer has refused, saying the tourist emailed after leaving the country to say she was not at fault.
statement: The police came, looked at both cars and the position, and gave her the fault. She signed the report too. I don't understand how an email from abroad can change that.

accounts.text: Collision at a roundabout. Vehicle 2 (rental, driven by a visitor) entered without giving way to vehicle 1 already on the roundabout. Fault: vehicle 2. Both drivers signed.
Our insured's driver disputes liability by email and has left the UAE. We are unable to accept the claim at this time.

whatHappened: A collision caused by the tourist, recorded in a signed police report. Her later email does not change the report.
damage: Policyholder's Accord: front-right wing and bumper, AED 14,500, repaired.
thirdParties: The rental company and its insurer
missing: Any formal objection to the police report filed by the tourist
inconsistencies: The tourist signed the report but now disputes fault by email
innocent: Visitors sometimes sign reports they do not fully understand
questions: Ask the rental insurer whether any formal objection to the police report was lodged
steps: Press the recovery on the police report, which assigned fault and was signed by both drivers
Ask the rental insurer to show any formal objection; an informal email is not one
Escalate through the UAE’s insurance dispute channels if the refusal continues
Recover her excess as part of the claim and keep her informed
assessment: Disputed only by the other side's informal objection. The signed police report supports full recovery.
action: Pursue the rental car's insurer on the police report and escalate if it keeps refusing.
outcomes: Rental insurer pays after escalation
Recovered through the dispute process with costs

title: Paid on the expert’s report, without the repair, and with VAT
type: Notional settlement on an expert report where VAT is claimed but not incurred
story: Our policyholder reversed into Ms Krüger's parked car in a supermarket car park in Hanover. Liability is accepted. She has claimed on the basis of her expert's report without having the car repaired: €6,300 net repair costs at brand-workshop rates, plus €1,197 VAT, the expert's fee and a flat sum for expenses. Her car is six years old and has been serviced at independent garages.
statement: I'll decide later whether to repair it or sell it. The expert's report says €7,497 including VAT, so that's what I'm claiming. Why would I get less than the report says?

accounts.text: Damage to the rear bumper, tailgate and rear panel. Repair costs at brand-workshop rates: €6,300 net, €1,197 VAT, €7,497 gross. Vehicle age 6 years. Service history: independent garages.
I was reversing out of the space and didn't see her car behind me. I accepted it on the spot and gave her my details.

whatHappened: A clear liability claim settled on a notional basis. VAT is not payable unless it is actually incurred, and brand-workshop rates may be replaced by a cheaper equivalent workshop for a car of this age and service history.
damage: Her VW Passat: rear bumper, tailgate and rear panel.
missing: Quotes from an equivalent independent workshop nearby
innocent: Claimants often expect the gross figure in an expert report to be paid in full
questions: Confirm whether she has had the car repaired or replaced
steps: Pay the net repair costs: under section 249(2) of the Civil Code, VAT is only payable if it is actually incurred
Consider referring her to an equivalent independent workshop’s rates, since the car is over three years old and not serviced at brand workshops, giving her a concrete, reachable alternative
Pay the expert’s fee and the usual flat sum for expenses
Tell her VAT will be paid if she later repairs and shows the invoice
assessment: Genuine claim, overstated by the VAT. A notional settlement pays net costs; VAT follows only if incurred.
action: Pay net repair costs, the expert's fee and the expense sum, and explain the VAT rule.
outcomes: Net costs paid; VAT paid later on a repair invoice
Settled at independent workshop rates after a concrete referral

title: €612 cut from the workshop invoice, and the 2024 rulings on who bears it
type: Liability insurer reduces a repair invoice as excessive
story: Our policyholder rear-ended Mr Brandt in Stuttgart. He had his car repaired at a workshop of his choice and sent the invoice of €5,940. The claims team paid €5,328, cutting €612 for a "workstation change" charge, extra cleaning and a paint mixing surcharge that its estimating system marks as unnecessary. Mr Brandt has not paid the workshop the balance and the workshop is pressing him.
statement: I took the car to a proper workshop and paid what I could. I can't check whether a workstation change was needed, I'm not a mechanic. Your insurer caused this, why am I stuck between you and the workshop?

accounts.text: Repair per expert report: €5,328. Additional items: workstation change €227, vehicle cleaning and disinfection €148, paint mixing surcharge €237. Total €5,940.
Paid €5,328. Deducted €612 as not necessary according to the estimating system. No contact with the workshop.

whatHappened: A genuine repair where the insurer cut items the claimant could not reasonably judge. Under the Federal Court of Justice rulings of January 2024, that workshop risk falls on the liable insurer.
damage: His Audi A3: rear bumper, boot lid and rear panel, repaired.
missing: Whether he has assigned his claim to the workshop
innocent: Estimating systems flag common surcharges whether or not they were justified on a particular job
questions: Ask whether he has paid the balance and whether he has assigned his claim to the workshop
steps: Pay the €612: following the Federal Court of Justice rulings of 16 January 2024, the claimant who had the repair done can claim the full invoice even if some items were unnecessary; if he has not paid the workshop, payment goes to the workshop
In return, ask him to assign any claims he has against the workshop for overcharging, and pursue the workshop directly if the items were unjustified
Note that if the workshop itself claims under an assignment from him, it cannot rely on the workshop risk rule
Update the deduction practice for repaired-vehicle claims
assessment: Genuine, and the deduction is against current case law. The insurer pays and takes over the dispute with the workshop.
action: Pay the balance to the workshop against an assignment of his claims, and pursue the workshop if warranted.
outcomes: Balance paid; workshop justifies two of the three items
Practice changed for repaired-vehicle invoices

title: Fourteen days of loss of use, and a second car in the garage
type: Loss of use compensation claimed while another household car was used
story: Our policyholder hit Mr Wagner's car at a junction in Leipzig; liability is accepted. He did not hire a car during the repair and claims loss of use compensation for 14 days at the table rate for his car's class. The expert estimated 5 working days for the repair. He started the repair nine days after the accident, after a holiday. His wife's Golf was available at home, and he says he used it to get to work.
statement: I couldn't use my own car for two weeks, so I'm owed for two weeks. Yes, I borrowed my wife's Golf for work, but that's her car, not mine. And the holiday was booked months ago, I couldn't take the car in before.

accounts.text: Repair duration: 5 working days. Vehicle drivable and safe to use until repair, with a damaged front wing and headlamp alignment to be checked.
Vehicle delivered for repair 9 days after the accident. Repair completed in 5 working days.

whatHappened: A genuine claim for loss of use, overstated: the car was drivable before the repair, the necessary repair period was 5 working days, and a second household car was available and used.
damage: His Skoda Octavia: front wing, bumper and headlamp. Drivable.
evidence: His statement about his wife's car
missing: Whether his wife needed her car during those days
inconsistencies: He claims 14 days; the car was drivable before the repair and the repair took 5 working days
indicators: Loss of use claimed for days when the car was drivable and another car was used
innocent: Many claimants believe loss of use runs from the accident until the car comes back
questions: Ask whether his wife went without her car during those days
steps: Limit loss of use to the necessary repair period, here about 5 working days, because the car was drivable before
Consider the household second car: if it was genuinely available to him without hardship to others, loss of use may not be due at all; if his wife went without, a payment for the repair days is fair
Explain the calculation clearly and pay the undisputed repair costs
assessment: Genuine claim, exaggerated in duration. At most the repair days are payable, and the second car may remove the loss entirely.
action: Pay the repair costs and, depending on the second car's availability, loss of use for the repair days only.
outcomes: Loss of use paid for 7 calendar days
Loss of use declined because the second car was freely available

title: Twenty-six reports by the same expert, all generous
type: Series of inflated expert reports on liability claims
story: A claimant in Duisburg says our policyholder scraped his rear bumper while parking. His expert's report prices a new bumper, a new rear panel section, blend painting of both rear doors and €900 of diminished value for a nine-year-old car with 180,000 km. The claimant's photos show a scrape on the bumper corner only. The same expert, lawyer and workshop appear in 26 claims against the insurer in nine months, all with similar line items.
statement: (Lawyer for the claimant) The report is by a certified independent expert and must be paid in full, together with the expert's fee and our fees. Your policyholder admitted fault.

accounts.text: Photos: a 15 cm scrape on the rear bumper corner, no visible deformation of the rear panel. Report: bumper replacement, rear panel section, blend painting of both rear doors, diminished value €900. Total €4,980 net.

26 liability claims in 9 months with the same expert, lawyer and workshop. In 21 of them, blend painting of adjacent panels and diminished value were claimed regardless of vehicle age or mileage. Average report value 2.4 times the insurer's own estimates for similar photos.

whatHappened: A minor genuine scrape, valued by an expert whose reports consistently inflate repairs and add diminished value where little or none can exist.
damage: BMW 3 Series: scrape to the rear bumper corner.
missing: A physical inspection by an independent expert instructed by the insurer
inconsistencies: The report replaces a rear panel the photos show undamaged
Diminished value claimed on a nine-year-old car with 180,000 km
indicators: Same expert, lawyer and workshop across 26 claims
Repairs priced well above the visible damage
Diminished value claimed regardless of age and mileage
innocent: Hidden damage behind a bumper corner is possible, which an inspection would reveal
questions: Ask to inspect the car before it is repaired
steps: Accept liability for the scrape, but not the report: instruct an independent expert to inspect the car
Pay the reasonable repair costs on the inspection; resist diminished value on a car of this age and mileage unless clearly shown
Review the 26 claims together with the counter-fraud team and consider a complaint to the expert’s certifying body
Do not allege fraud in correspondence before the review is complete
assessment: Potential fraud by inflation across a series of claims. The scrape is real; the report's scope is not supported by the photos.
action: Inspect independently, pay the reasonable cost, and review the expert's claims as a group.
outcomes: Settled at €1,150 after inspection
Expert’s certification withdrawn after the group review

title: A cyclist hurt in Lyon, and eight months to make an offer
type: Injured cyclist awaiting the compulsory compensation offer
story: Our policyholder turned across a cyclist, Ms Fontaine, in Lyon on 10 January. She suffered a fractured tibia and a broken wrist and has had two operations. Her doctors say her condition is not yet consolidated. It is now 25 August and no compensation offer has been sent to her. The file note says the handler was waiting for consolidation before making any offer.
statement: I've been off work since January. I've had two operations and physiotherapy three times a week. Nobody from the insurance has made me any offer, not even something provisional. My lawyer says there are rules about this.

accounts.text: Fracture of the left tibia with internal fixation, fracture of the right wrist. Second operation in May. Not consolidated; consolidation expected in 6 to 9 months.
Liability accepted. Awaiting consolidation before making an offer. Interim payment of €3,000 made in March.

whatHappened: A cyclist injured by our policyholder, with liability accepted. The insurer has wrongly waited for consolidation and is close to the legal deadline for an offer.
damage: Fractured tibia and wrist, two operations, off work for over seven months. Bicycle destroyed.
missing: A medical assessment for a provisional offer
Her loss of earnings documents
innocent: Waiting for consolidation is a common misunderstanding; the law requires a provisional offer meanwhile
questions: Ask her lawyer for her earnings documents
steps: Make a provisional offer now: the Code des assurances requires an offer to an injured victim within 8 months of the accident, which falls on 10 September, provisional if the condition is not consolidated
Base it on a medical assessment and her documented losses so far, with further interim payments if needed
Diary the final offer: it must follow within 5 months of the insurer learning of consolidation
Note the sanction: a late or manifestly insufficient offer attracts interest at double the legal rate
assessment: Genuine and serious, liability accepted. The insurer must make a provisional offer before 10 September rather than wait for consolidation.
action: Arrange a medical assessment and make a reasoned provisional offer before the 8-month deadline.
outcomes: Provisional offer made on 5 September; final offer after consolidation
Deadline missed; double interest applied by the court

title: Hit by an uninsured driver, with third-party cover only
type: Collision with an identified uninsured driver; compensation through the guarantee fund
story: Policyholder's car was hit at a junction in Marseille by a driver who ran a stop sign. The police identified the other driver and found he had no insurance. Policyholder has third-party-only cover, so his own policy does not pay for his car. He asked his insurer who will pay for the €3,800 of damage.
statement: The police said he had no insurance at all and they seized his car. I only have third-party cover because my car is old. Surely I'm not the one who has to pay when he broke the law?

accounts.text: Vehicle B failed to stop at a stop sign and struck vehicle A. Driver of vehicle B identified; no valid insurance; vehicle impounded. Driver of vehicle A not at fault.
Third-party liability (responsabilité civile) only. Legal protection option included.

whatHappened: A not-at-fault collision with an identified, uninsured driver. His own third-party policy does not cover his car; the national guarantee fund compensates victims of uninsured drivers.
damage: His Clio: front-left wing, bumper and headlamp, €3,800.
missing: The guarantee fund claim form
innocent: Owners of older cars often choose third-party cover without realising it leaves them exposed to uninsured drivers
questions: Confirm whether he has started a claim with the guarantee fund
steps: Explain that his third-party policy does not pay for his own car
Guide him to claim from the guarantee fund for victims of uninsured drivers (FGAO), within its time limits and subject to its own conditions and any deductible
Use his legal protection option to help him with the guarantee fund claim and any action against the driver
Record that he was not at fault so his bonus is not affected
assessment: Genuine and not at fault. The remedy is the guarantee fund, with help from his legal protection cover.
action: Explain the position, help him claim from the FGAO, and protect his bonus.
outcomes: Paid by the guarantee fund less its deductible
Legal protection recovers the deductible from the driver

title: Declared twelve days late because of a funeral abroad
type: Claim declared after the contractual period, with no prejudice to the insurer
story: Policyholder had a low-speed collision in a Toulouse car park and completed a joint accident report (constat amiable) with the other driver at the scene. She flew to Algeria the next day for a family funeral and declared the claim to her insurer twelve days after the accident. The claims clerk has proposed refusing the claim for late declaration.
statement: My uncle died and I left the next morning. I had the constat in my bag the whole time. I declared it the day after I got back. Nothing has changed, the other driver signed everything, and my car hasn't been repaired.

accounts.text: Signed by both drivers at the scene. Vehicle B reversing from a space into vehicle A which was passing behind. Both drivers' insurers and details complete.
Declaration received 12 days after the accident; contract requires 5 working days. Propose refusal for late declaration (déchéance).

whatHappened: A genuine car park collision with a complete joint report. The late declaration had a good reason and caused the insurer no harm.
damage: Her Peugeot 208: rear door and wheel arch, €1,900.
thirdParties: The other driver and their insurer
missing: Confirmation from the other insurer that it has the same constat
innocent: A bereavement abroad is an obvious reason for delay
questions: Confirm the car is still unrepaired for the assessor
steps: Do not refuse: under the Code des assurances, a late declaration can only lead to loss of cover if the insurer proves the delay caused it prejudice, and there is none here
Process the claim under the joint report and the inter-insurer agreements
Correct the clerk’s proposal and remind the team of the prejudice requirement
assessment: Genuine and payable. The delay is explained and harmless; refusing would be unlawful.
action: Accept the declaration and handle the claim on the constat.
outcomes: Claim handled normally; other insurer bears the cost under the constat
Team briefed on late declarations

title: Half at fault, charged the full malus
type: Complaint about the bonus-malus applied after shared liability
story: Policyholder and another driver both changed lanes into each other on a ring road in Nantes in the rain. The insurers settled liability 50/50. At renewal, his bonus-malus coefficient went up by 25%, the increase for a fully responsible claim. He complained in writing six weeks ago and has had only an automatic acknowledgment. He has asked how to go to the insurance mediator.
statement: Your own letter says liability was shared fifty-fifty. My friend who works in insurance says half liability means half the increase. I've written once and heard nothing. I want this corrected and I want to know how to complain properly.

accounts.text: Following the inter-insurer agreement, liability for this claim is shared: 50% your responsibility.
Bonus-malus coefficient: previous 0.68, new 0.85 (increase of 25% for a responsible claim).

whatHappened: A shared-liability collision rated as if he were fully responsible. The rules give half the increase for partial responsibility.
damage: His Mégane: front-right wing and door, repaired.
thirdParties: The other driver and their insurer
missing: The insurer’s substantive reply to the complaint
inconsistencies: Liability was settled at 50%; the malus applied was the full 25%
innocent: Rating systems sometimes apply a full malus by default when liability is entered as "responsible"
questions: Check how the liability split was entered in the rating system
steps: Correct the coefficient: for a partly responsible claim the increase is 12.5%, not 25%, giving 0.76 after rounding down to two decimals
Refund the premium overcharged and send a substantive written reply
Explain his rights: the insurer should answer complaints within two months, and he can refer the matter to La Médiation de l’Assurance if he remains unhappy
Check for other policyholders affected by the same rating error
assessment: Disputed on its face but clear on the rules: shared liability carries half the malus. The complaint should be upheld.
action: Correct the coefficient, refund the difference and reply substantively with his mediation rights.
outcomes: Coefficient corrected and premium refunded
Rating error found on other shared-liability claims and fixed

title: Torched outside his shop during the unrest
type: Vehicle burnt during public unrest; special risks cover applies
story: Policyholder's bakkie was set alight by a crowd during violent unrest in Pietermaritzburg while it was parked outside his hardware shop. A claims handler has drafted a rejection under the comprehensive section's exclusion for riot, strike and civil commotion. The policy schedule shows a SASRIA premium charged every month for special risks cover on the vehicle.
statement: The crowd came down the street throwing things and setting cars alight, I locked myself in the shop. By the time it was safe the bakkie was burnt to the frame. The police came the next day and gave me a case number. I pay for SASRIA every month, it's on my statement.

accounts.text: Public violence and malicious damage to property during unrest in the area. Several vehicles and shops set alight. Complainant's vehicle burnt while parked. Case registered.
Comprehensive motor. Exclusion: riot, strike, civil commotion and public disorder. SASRIA special risks cover: included, premium charged monthly.

whatHappened: The vehicle was destroyed in public unrest. That is excluded from the comprehensive section but is exactly what the SASRIA cover on his schedule is for.
damage: Toyota Hilux burnt out, total loss; retail value about R310,000.
missing: Any news or police reports confirming unrest in that street on that date, if SASRIA asks
innocent: Handlers who see the riot exclusion may not check the SASRIA section of the schedule
questions: Confirm the date and street against the reports of unrest
steps: Do not reject: the riot exclusion removes the loss from the comprehensive section, but the SASRIA cover on his schedule responds to riot and public disorder
Submit the claim under the SASRIA cover with the SAPS case number and evidence of the unrest, within the required time limits
Explain the process to him and keep him informed
Correct the draft rejection
assessment: Genuine and covered under SASRIA. The draft rejection looks only at the comprehensive exclusion.
action: Process the claim under the SASRIA cover and withdraw the rejection.
outcomes: Paid under SASRIA as a total loss
Handler guidance updated to check special risks cover

title: A pothole reported five weeks earlier on the municipal app
type: Pothole damage with a possible recovery from the municipality
story: Policyholder hit a deep, water-filled pothole on a municipal road in Pretoria at night, damaging two rims, two tyres and the front suspension. The claim is R18,400. A resident's report about the same pothole was logged on the municipality's service app five weeks before, with a reference number and a photo. The insurer is paying the claim and is considering recovery from the municipality.
statement: It was raining and the hole was full of water, it looked like a puddle. The bang was huge and two tyres went flat. A neighbour showed me that people had reported that exact pothole weeks ago and nothing was done.

accounts.text: Service request logged five weeks before the incident: "large pothole, danger to vehicles", with a photo and location matching the incident. Status: open, not attended.
Two alloy rims, two tyres, front left lower control arm and wheel alignment. R18,400.

whatHappened: A genuine pothole impact on a defect the municipality had been told about and left unrepaired.
damage: Two rims, two tyres, front suspension arm; R18,400.
evidence: Photos of the pothole at night
missing: Measurements of the pothole
Whether warning signs were placed
innocent: A water-filled pothole at night looks like a puddle, so hitting it is not careless driving
questions: Ask her for daylight photos and measurements of the pothole
steps: Pay her claim under the comprehensive cover, less her excess
Send the municipality written notice of the claim within six months, as the law on legal proceedings against organs of state requires, or the recovery may be lost
Use the service request to show the municipality knew of the danger and did nothing for five weeks
Include her excess in the recovery
assessment: Genuine, with a good recovery case because the defect had been reported. The six-month notice is the key deadline.
action: Pay the claim and serve notice on the municipality in time, using the prior report as evidence.
outcomes: Municipality settles after notice and the service request evidence
Recovery lost because notice was sent after six months

title: Hijacked at nine, but the tracker was cut at twenty to
type: Reported hijacking contradicted by tracking data
story: Policyholder reported that his Toyota Hilux was hijacked at gunpoint at 21:00 at a traffic light in Midrand. He opened a SAPS case at 23:30. The tracking company's data shows the vehicle drove to an address in Soshanguve at 20:15, stopped there, and the tracking unit raised a tamper alert at 20:40 before going offline. The Soshanguve address is registered to his brother-in-law.
statement: Two men with a gun came to my window at the robot and told me to get out. They drove off with the bakkie. I was so shocked I sat on the pavement for an hour before I went to the police. I don't know anything about Soshanguve, maybe the tracker is wrong.

accounts.text: 19:55 departed the policyholder's home. 20:15 arrived at an address in Soshanguve; ignition off. 20:40 tamper alert: unit power disconnected. No further signal. No movement recorded towards Midrand.
Complainant reports a hijacking at about 21:00 at an intersection in Midrand. Case opened at 23:30. No witnesses recorded. Intersection camera footage requested.

whatHappened: The bakkie was driven to his brother-in-law's address and the tracker was disconnected there before the time of the reported hijacking.
damage: Toyota Hilux reported hijacked; value about R480,000.
missing: Intersection camera footage in Midrand
His phone location data for the evening
inconsistencies: He says the bakkie was taken in Midrand at 21:00; the tracker shows it at a Soshanguve address with the unit disconnected at 20:40
indicators: Tracker disconnected at a relative’s address before the reported hijacking
Two-and-a-half hour delay before the police report
He denies knowing the address
innocent: Tracking units can misreport after tampering, but the tamper alert itself came before the reported time
questions: Ask him to account for the vehicle’s journey to Soshanguve
Ask the brother-in-law whether the bakkie was at his house
steps: Interview him with the tracking data, in line with the policy’s claims conditions
Get the Midrand intersection footage through SAPS
Do not settle while the tracking data is unexplained
If the data stands, reject the claim and report the false statement to SAPS
assessment: Potential fraud with strong data: the vehicle and tracker were at a relative's address before the reported hijacking.
action: Investigate with the tracking evidence and footage before any decision.
outcomes: Bakkie found at a scrapyard linked to the brother-in-law; claim rejected
Claim withdrawn after the interview

title: Rejected for no tracker, a condition nobody mentioned on the phone
type: Theft claim rejected for a tracking device condition not disclosed at sale
story: Policyholder's Toyota Fortuner was stolen from a shopping centre parking lot in Johannesburg. The claim was rejected because the policy requires an approved tracking device for vehicles of that model and value, and none was fitted. He bought the policy by phone. The call recording shows the sales agent did not mention the tracking condition. The policy documents emailed afterwards include it in the schedule's endorsements.
statement: The agent asked about my car, my address and whether I park in a garage. Nothing about a tracker. I would have fitted one, it's a few hundred rand a month. Now I've lost a car I'm still paying for. I'm going to the ombud.

accounts.text: Eighteen-minute call. Questions on vehicle, overnight parking, driver history. No mention of a tracking device requirement. Agent says: "You're fully comprehensive, you're covered for theft and hijacking."
Theft and hijacking cover for this vehicle is conditional on an approved tracking device being fitted and active. Documents emailed the day after the sale.

whatHappened: A genuine theft. The tracking condition is in the documents but was not disclosed in the sale, and the agent described the cover as complete.
damage: Toyota Fortuner stolen; value about R560,000; finance outstanding.
missing: Whether he read the emailed documents
Whether a tracker would likely have led to recovery
inconsistencies: The agent said he was covered for theft; the documents make theft cover conditional on a tracker
innocent: Customers buying by phone rely on what the agent says
questions: Ask whether he received and read the emailed schedule
steps: Review the rejection under the treating customers fairly principles and the Policyholder Protection Rules: a material condition that was not disclosed at sale, with the agent stating full theft cover, is unlikely to be upheld by the ombud
Consider paying the claim, or at least a fair settlement, rather than relying on the endorsement
Respond to his complaint in writing with reasons and explain his right to approach the ombud
Fix the sales script so material conditions are disclosed on the call
assessment: Disputed, but the sales failure weighs heavily against the insurer. Relying on an undisclosed condition is likely to be found unfair.
action: Reconsider the rejection, likely pay, and fix the sales disclosure.
outcomes: Claim paid after internal review; sales script changed
Ombud recommends payment in full

title: A side-swipe in Johor Bahru, and two versions at the merge
type: Collision in Malaysia on a Singapore policy, with a disputed lane merge
story: Policyholder drove his Singapore-registered car to Johor Bahru for the weekend. Where two lanes merge after a traffic light, his car and a Malaysian car side-swiped each other. Both drivers made police reports in Johor within 24 hours, each blaming the other. The Malaysian driver has claimed against the policyholder's Singapore insurer for repairs and three weeks of car rental. The policyholder reported the accident to his insurer the next morning.
statement: My lane was the one that continued, his lane ended with arrows to merge. He tried to squeeze in at the last moment and hit my front door. I made the police report at the station near the checkpoint before driving back. I have a front dashcam.

accounts.text: Complainant states the Singapore car moved left into his lane while merging and hit his car. Complainant's car damaged on the right side.

Front camera: the policyholder's lane continues; arrows painted in the left lane indicate it ends. The Malaysian car comes alongside from the ending lane and moves right; contact at the policyholder's front-left door. The policyholder's car stays within its lane markings.

whatHappened: The Malaysian driver merged from an ending lane into the policyholder's continuing lane. The dashcam supports the policyholder.
damage: Policyholder's Mazda 3: front-left door and wing. Malaysian car: right-side doors.
thirdParties: The Malaysian driver and his insurer
missing: The Malaysian car's own insurer and any dashcam
Rental invoices
inconsistencies: Each driver says the other moved into their lane
innocent: Unfamiliar road markings across the border cause genuine misunderstandings
questions: Ask the Malaysian driver’s side for any footage and the rental invoices
steps: Confirm the policy’s geographical area covers West Malaysia, and that both reports were made in time
Deny the third-party claim on the dashcam evidence, or negotiate a split if the other side produces contrary footage
Handle the policyholder’s own damage under his cover and pursue the Malaysian driver’s insurer for recovery
Use a Malaysian adjuster for the third-party side if needed
assessment: Disputed, but the dashcam and the lane markings favour the policyholder. The Malaysian driver merged from the ending lane.
action: Defend the third-party claim on the footage and recover the policyholder's losses.
outcomes: Malaysian insurer accepts liability after viewing the footage
Settled 70/30 in the policyholder’s favour

title: Rear-ended by his friend, with a dent from three months ago
type: Friends’ collision used to claim for old damage
story: Policyholder Daniel Koh reported that he rear-ended his friend Jason Lim's car at low speed in a Jurong car park. Both reported the accident under the Motor Claims Framework and Mr Lim has claimed S$6,900 against Mr Koh's policy. The damage includes a rust-pitted dent in the bumper and a tail lamp with dirt inside its crack. The workshop is run by Mr Koh's cousin. A photo on Mr Lim's social media from three months earlier shows the same dent.
statement: (Daniel Koh, our policyholder) I was slow, maybe 10 km/h, and I tapped Jason's car when he stopped suddenly. We're friends so we went to my cousin's workshop, he gives good prices. I told him to claim from my insurance since it was my fault.

accounts.text: Fresh contact marks on the bumper corner consistent with a low-speed tap. Separate dent with rust pitting in the paint, older than the incident. Tail lamp crack contains dirt and moisture. Estimated fresh damage S$1,300.
Photo posted by Mr Lim three months before the incident, showing his car at a car meet. The dent on the rear bumper is visible in the same position.

whatHappened: A real low-speed tap between friends, used to put older damage on the policyholder's insurance.
damage: Fresh contact marks on the bumper corner. Older dent and cracked tail lamp included in the S$6,900 claim.
missing: Car park CCTV
The workshop's photos before repair
inconsistencies: The claim includes a dent visible in a photo taken three months before the incident
indicators: Claim between friends repaired at a relative’s workshop
Old damage included in the estimate
Claim far above the fresh damage
innocent: Friends often use a familiar workshop, and the workshop may have quoted everything it saw
questions: Ask Mr Lim to explain the dent in the earlier photo
Ask the car park for CCTV
steps: Offer to pay the fresh damage only, about S$1,300, and decline the older items with the photo as the reason
Put the photo to both men in interviews
Refer to the fraud team if they persist with the full amount
Note the link between the policyholder and the workshop
assessment: Potential fraud: a genuine minor tap with older damage added, arranged between friends and a related workshop.
action: Pay only the fresh damage and investigate if the full claim is pressed.
outcomes: Claim reduced to S$1,300 and accepted
Referred after the claimant insists on the full amount

title: "I was driving," until the workshop camera showed her son
type: Wrong driver given to avoid the young and inexperienced driver excesses
story: Policyholder reported that she hit a bollard while parking at a condominium in Tampines. Her policy has a S$600 excess, plus additional excesses of S$2,500 each for a young driver and an inexperienced driver. The car's own camera and the condominium's CCTV show her 22-year-old son, who passed his test a year ago, driving. When shown the footage she admitted it and apologized.
statement: I panicked. My son is careful, he just misjudged the bollard. I knew there was a big excess for young drivers and I thought it was a small accident, it wouldn't matter who drove. I'm sorry, I should have told the truth.

accounts.text: A young man drives the car into the bay and strikes the bollard. He gets out from the driver's seat. The policyholder arrives ten minutes later.

Excess: S$600. Additional excess S$2,500 where the driver is under 27, and S$2,500 where the driver has held a licence for less than 2 years. Named drivers: policyholder only. Unnamed drivers permitted with the additional excesses.

whatHappened: A genuine bollard strike by her son. She named herself as the driver to avoid S$5,000 of additional excesses, then admitted it.
damage: Toyota Corolla Altis: front bumper and grille, S$2,900.
missing: The son's own account of the incident
inconsistencies: Her report named herself; the footage shows her son driving
indicators: False statement about the driver to reduce the excess
innocent: A parent protecting a child in a moment of panic, corrected before payment
questions: Confirm the son’s licence date
steps: Apply the correct excesses for the actual driver: S$600 plus both additional excesses; with damage of S$2,900, the excesses exceed the loss, so nothing is payable
Record the false statement and treat it seriously: a deliberate misstatement in a claim can justify refusing the claim and may affect future cover
Warn her in writing, as the statement was corrected before any payment
Offer to add her son as a named driver at the correct premium
assessment: Suspicious conduct on a genuine incident: a deliberate but corrected misstatement. Applying the correct excesses resolves the claim.
action: Apply the correct excesses, record and warn about the false statement, and update the named drivers.
outcomes: No payment due after excesses; warning issued
Insurer declines to renew after a second misstatement

title: A delivery rider’s S$85,000 claim and the online assessment tool
type: Injury claim valued above the court’s online assessment range
story: Our policyholder turned right across a delivery rider at a junction in Tampines. The rider fractured his wrist. His lawyers claim S$85,000, including six months of lost earnings. The court's online assessment tool, using past cases, suggests a range for the wrist injury well below that and a liability split favouring the rider. The delivery platform's records show he resumed deliveries three weeks after the accident.
statement: (Through his lawyers) Our client could not work for six months and still has pain gripping the handlebars. He supports his parents. The insurer's driver turned without looking.

accounts.text: Liability: right-turning car mainly at fault; rider may bear a small share for speed. Quantum for a wrist fracture with good recovery: a range far below the amount claimed. Loss of earnings to be proved by records.
Account inactive for 21 days after the accident date. Deliveries resumed thereafter at about 80% of previous weekly volume, returning to normal within two months.

whatHappened: A genuine injury mainly caused by our policyholder. The claimed earnings loss is overstated: he returned to work after three weeks.
damage: Fractured wrist treated with a cast; physiotherapy. Motorcycle repaired.
missing: A specialist report on any lasting grip weakness
inconsistencies: Six months of lost earnings claimed; platform records show work resumed after three weeks
indicators: Earnings claim contradicted by platform records
innocent: He may have worked in pain at reduced volume, which is a real loss for a shorter period
questions: Ask for his earnings before and after the accident from the platform
steps: Accept that liability rests mainly on the policyholder
Value the injury using the online assessment range and the medical evidence
Pay lost earnings for the three weeks off and the reduced volume afterwards, on the platform records
Make a reasoned offer and use the tool’s range in negotiation or mediation
assessment: Genuine injury, overstated claim. The assessment tool and the platform records set a fair range well below the demand.
action: Offer within the tool's range with proven earnings losses.
outcomes: Settled at S$31,000
Resolved at court-assisted mediation within the tool’s range

title: Assessed at €12,000 by the Injuries Resolution Board, and a handler who wants to reject it
type: Decision on a statutory injury assessment within the guidelines
story: Our policyholder rear-ended Ms Byrne's car in Galway. She suffered a neck injury and a wrist sprain. The Injuries Resolution Board assessed her claim at €12,000 under the Personal Injuries Guidelines, supported by a medical report. The handler wants to reject the assessment because "whiplash is overpaid". If the insurer rejects it, the Board will issue an authorisation and she can sue.
statement: (Through her solicitor) Our client has accepted the assessment. She has had physiotherapy for five months and still has symptoms in her wrist. If your client rejects it we will issue proceedings.

accounts.text: Neck soft-tissue injury, substantial recovery within six months. Wrist sprain with persisting symptoms at five months, prognosis for recovery within twelve months. No pre-existing problems.
General damages assessed under the Personal Injuries Guidelines for the dominant wrist injury with an uplift for the neck injury, plus special damages. Total €12,000. Claimant has accepted.

whatHappened: A genuine injury fairly assessed under the Guidelines. Rejecting it would mean litigation with higher costs and little prospect of a lower award.
damage: Neck soft-tissue injury and wrist sprain. Car damage settled separately.
missing: Any medical evidence the handler relies on for a lower figure
innocent: Handlers sometimes judge awards by pre-Guidelines experience
questions: Ask the handler what in the medical evidence supports a lower figure
steps: Check the assessment against the Guidelines brackets for the dominant injury and the medical prognosis
Accept within the time allowed if, as it appears, the assessment is within the Guidelines
Explain to the business that rejection leads to an authorisation, court proceedings and legal costs that will likely exceed any saving
Reject only with specific medical or factual grounds, recorded on file
assessment: Genuine and fairly assessed. Accepting the assessment is the sensible and fair outcome.
action: Accept the €12,000 assessment within the time allowed.
outcomes: Assessment accepted and paid
Rejected, then settled in court at €13,500 plus costs

title: Rear-ended in Christchurch, and she wants him to pay for her neck
type: Injury claim against the at-fault driver where ACC covers personal injury
story: Policyholder was rear-ended at lights in Christchurch. She has a neck injury and two weeks off work. She has asked her insurer to claim compensation for her injury and lost wages from the other driver, along with the repairs to her car. The other driver admitted fault and is insured.
statement: He was on his phone, he admitted it. My neck still hurts and I lost two weeks' pay. In Australia my cousin got money from the other driver's insurance for her injuries. Why can't I?

accounts.text: I looked down at my phone and went into the back of her car. My fault completely. My insurer's details are attached.
Neck sprain. Two weeks off work. ACC claim lodged by the GP on the day of the consultation.

whatHappened: A genuine not-at-fault collision. Her injury is covered by ACC, which bars suing for personal injury compensation; her car damage is claimed from the other driver's insurer.
damage: Her Corolla: rear bumper and boot, NZ$3,200. Neck sprain, two weeks off work.
thirdParties: The other driver and his insurer
evidence: GP note with the ACC claim
missing: ACC’s decision on weekly compensation
innocent: Rules in Australia are different, which is a common source of confusion
questions: Ask whether ACC has confirmed her weekly compensation
steps: Explain that ACC covers her injury, treatment and lost earnings on a no-fault basis, and that New Zealand law bars suing for compensation for a personal injury covered by ACC
Claim her car repairs and excess from the other driver’s insurer, or pay under her own policy and recover
Help her follow up the ACC weekly compensation
assessment: Genuine and not at fault. The injury goes through ACC; the property damage goes against the other driver's insurer.
action: Explain ACC, and recover her vehicle damage from the at-fault driver's insurer.
outcomes: ACC pays weekly compensation; car repaired and recovered
She accepts the explanation after a call

title: A pedestrian in Osaka, and the compulsory cover’s ¥1.2 million ceiling
type: Serious pedestrian injury exceeding the compulsory insurance limit
story: Our policyholder struck a 70-year-old pedestrian, Mr Sato, at a crossing in Osaka in the rain. He suffered a fractured hip and has been in hospital for six weeks. Medical costs so far are ¥3.4 million. The policyholder has both the compulsory automobile liability insurance and our voluntary insurance. The family has asked who will pay the hospital and whether they need a lawyer.
statement: (Mr Sato's daughter) My father was on the crossing with the green light. The hospital is asking us for payment. He may need care at home after this. We don't know which insurance pays what.

accounts.text: Pedestrian struck on a crossing while the pedestrian signal was green. Driver states rain on the windscreen reduced visibility. Driver at fault.
Hip fracture, surgery and six weeks of inpatient care. Costs to date ¥3,400,000. Rehabilitation expected for several months.

whatHappened: A serious pedestrian injury caused by our policyholder. The costs already exceed the compulsory insurance limit for injury, so the voluntary insurance must cover the rest.
damage: Fractured hip, surgery, long rehabilitation.
missing: A prognosis for long-term care needs
innocent: Rain on the windscreen at a crossing explains, but does not excuse, the driver not seeing him
questions: Ask the family about his care needs after discharge
steps: Offer one-stop handling: the voluntary insurer deals with the family and the hospital for the whole claim and recovers the compulsory portion from the compulsory insurer
Pay the hospital directly so the family is not asked for payment
Explain that the compulsory cover pays injury losses up to ¥1.2 million and the voluntary insurance pays above that
Assess consolation money and future care fairly, and tell the family they may consult a lawyer
assessment: Genuine and serious; the policyholder is at fault. The voluntary insurance carries most of the cost above the compulsory limit.
action: Take on one-stop handling, pay the hospital directly, and plan for care costs.
outcomes: Settled after rehabilitation including home care costs
Family instructs a lawyer; settled at court standards

title: A friendly report signed by both drivers, and no offer after six weeks
type: Direct compensation claim handled outside the statutory offer period
story: Policyholder was not at fault in a junction collision in Milan and claimed under the direct compensation system, which means her own insurer handles the claim. She submitted a joint accident report (CAI) signed by both drivers on 2 March, with photos and a repair estimate. On 15 April she had received no offer and no reasons. She has complained to the insurer and says she will go to the regulator.
statement: The other driver signed that it was his fault. I sent everything the same day. I've had no offer, no refusal, nothing. I've read that there are deadlines. My car has been parked for six weeks.

accounts.text: Signed by both drivers on 2 March. Vehicle B failed to give way at a junction and struck vehicle A. Vehicle B driver accepts responsibility.
Claim received with the signed CAI, photos and estimate on 2 March. Inspection done 10 March. No offer or reasoned refusal issued. Complaint received 15 April.

whatHappened: A straightforward not-at-fault claim with a CAI signed by both drivers, left without an offer past the statutory period.
damage: Her Fiat 500: front-right wing and bumper, estimate €2,300.
thirdParties: The other driver and his insurer
missing: Any reason recorded for the delay
innocent: Inspection backlogs after holidays can delay offers, but do not extend the legal period
questions: Check whether other direct compensation claims are overdue
steps: Make the offer now: under article 148 of the Code, the insurer must make a reasoned offer or refusal within 30 days where the CAI is signed by both drivers (60 days otherwise, 90 for injuries)
Pay interest for the delay and answer her complaint within the regulator’s time limit
Tell her she can complain to IVASS if she is not satisfied
Fix the cause of the delay
assessment: Genuine and overdue. The 30-day period for a jointly signed report has long passed.
action: Make the offer with interest, answer the complaint, and explain the IVASS route.
outcomes: Offer accepted within a week of the complaint
IVASS complaint leads to a sanction for repeated delays

title: A fourteen-year-old Ibiza worth €1,800 and a repair bill of €4,200
type: Third-party claim where repair costs far exceed the car’s market value
story: Our policyholder hit the side of Ms Ruiz's 14-year-old Seat Ibiza in Valencia. Liability is accepted. The repair estimate is €4,200. The car's market value (valor venal) is about €1,800. She insists on repair, saying the car is in excellent condition, has low mileage and she cannot find a replacement for that money. The handler has offered €1,800.
statement: I've looked after that car for fourteen years and it has 90,000 km. For €1,800 I'd get a wreck. I use it every day to take my mother to the hospital. It was his fault, why should I lose my car?

accounts.text: Market value of a comparable Seat Ibiza of this age: about €1,800. Vehicle in above-average condition, 90,000 km, full service history.
Two doors, B-pillar repair and paint: €4,200.

whatHappened: A genuine claim where repair costs more than twice the market value. Spanish practice usually pays market value plus an uplift for the owner's loss when repair is disproportionate, but the gap and the car's condition are argued.
damage: Seat Ibiza: two doors and B-pillar.
missing: Quotes for comparable cars in similar condition
innocent: Owners of well-kept older cars face real replacement difficulty
questions: Ask her for listings of comparable cars in similar condition
steps: Do not stop at the bare market value: offer the market value plus an uplift for the owner’s loss (valor de afección), as Spanish practice commonly allows where repair is disproportionate
Consider whether the repair is truly disproportionate given the car’s condition and her daily need; courts may allow repair where the cost is not excessive in context
Make a reasoned offer explaining the basis, and keep the option of paying for repair if the difference is modest
assessment: Genuine, with a real dispute about measure. €1,800 alone undercompensates her; a reasoned uplift or a negotiated repair is fairer.
action: Offer market value plus an afección uplift with reasons, and consider repair if the gap narrows.
outcomes: Settled at €2,700 including the uplift
Agreed to pay for repair after she finds no comparable car

title: Rear-ended on the Federal Highway, and his no-claim discount on the line
type: Own-damage knock-for-knock claim where the other insurer disputes liability
story: Policyholder was rear-ended in heavy rain on the Federal Highway in Kuala Lumpur. To get his car repaired quickly he claimed under his own policy through the knock-for-knock arrangement, which protects his no-claim discount when he is not at fault. The other driver's insurer now disputes liability, saying the policyholder braked suddenly for no reason. The policyholder's dashcam shows a motorcycle cutting in front of him.
statement: A motorcycle cut across in front of me in the rain and I had to brake. The car behind was too close. I made the police report the same evening. I chose the knock-for-knock claim so I wouldn't lose my 55% discount.

accounts.text: Motorcycle cuts across from the left lane without signalling about 15 metres ahead. Policyholder brakes firmly; the car stops. About 1.5 seconds later the rear impact occurs.
Our insured states your insured braked suddenly and without reason. We do not accept liability under the knock-for-knock arrangement.

whatHappened: A rear-end collision after the policyholder braked for a motorcyclist. A following driver should keep a safe distance, so liability rests mainly with the other driver.
damage: His Honda City: rear bumper, boot and tail lamps, RM 5,600.
thirdParties: The other driver and his insurer
missing: The other driver's police report
inconsistencies: The other driver says he braked for no reason; the dashcam shows a motorcycle cutting in
innocent: From behind, a driver may not see why the car in front braked
questions: Ask for the other driver's police report
steps: Repair the car under the knock-for-knock claim and keep his no-claim discount protected while liability is resolved
Send the dashcam footage to the other insurer: braking for a hazard does not shift fault from a driver who failed to keep a safe distance
Pursue recovery under the knock-for-knock arrangement and escalate through the industry dispute process if refused
assessment: Disputed only on a weak point. The footage shows a real hazard, and the following driver was too close.
action: Protect his discount, share the footage, and recover from the other insurer.
outcomes: Other insurer accepts after viewing the footage; discount protected
Resolved through the industry dispute process in his favour
